title: Vaccine clinic opens after four teens infected in measles outbreak
text:
A temporary vaccination service has been set up for a school community in Adelaide's southern suburbs after four students tested positive for measles.

SA Health issued a measles outbreak alert yesterday after three teenagers contracted the infectious disease.

The health authority said those cases were linked to a positive infection in another teenager reported on September 14, who had returned from overseas.

"My team and I are very concerned about this outbreak … we don't normally see such amount of spread," the state's chief public health officer Nicola Spurrier said.

"It is one of the most infectious communicable diseases that we know about and in an unvaccinated population, one case on average spreads to 14 other people.

"We're not sure if there are other cases brewing in the school."

Professor Nicola Spurrier reminds people who may have attended exposure sites to consider whether they have been immunised. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

SA Health and the Holdfast Bay Council have established a temporary vaccination clinic for the Brighton Secondary School community, which will operate at the Brighton Masonic Hall on 1 Commercial Road at Brighton from 2pm-6pm on Friday.

South Australia now has eight cases this year, the highest since 2016.

SA Health said the teenagers were in multiple locations while infectious, including a school and a shopping centre.

Exposure sites

Kilburn: Costco on Thursday, September 17 from 1:30pm–3:15pm and Costco Petrol Station from 2:45pm–3:35pm.

Hyde Park: El Mexicano Restaurant on Thursday, September 17 from 6:30pm–9:00pm and St Louis cafe from 8:30pm–9:30pm.

Oaklands Park: Kmart Westfield Marion on Friday, September 18 from 1:30pm–6:00pm and Monday, September 21 from 3:15pm-7:00pm.

Morphett Vale Stadium on Saturday, September 19 from 2:40pm–5:00pm

North Brighton: Brighton Secondary School on Friday 18 September from 9:00am–3:00pm.

Exposure sites from the September 14 case

Singapore Airlines Flight SQ431 from Maldives to Singapore on Monday, September 7 at 1:10pm.

Singapore Airlines Flight SQ279 from Singapore to Adelaide on Monday, September 7 at 11:20pm.

Adelaide Airport on Tuesday, September 8 from 7:20am–9:30am.

North Brighton: Brighton Secondary School on Wednesday, September 9 from 8:45am–3:45pm and Thursday, September 10 from 3:15pm–4:30pm.

Adelaide Metro Bus 265 travelling from Adelaide CBD to Marion Centre Stop 29 to terminus on Thursday, September 10 from 4:30pm–5:00pm.

Measles takes seven to 18 days to incubate and two weeks for a rash to appear.

The virus spreads by respiratory aerosols — such as through coughing and sneezing, or through touching surfaces — which remain a risk to others for up to 30 minutes after the person has left the area.

Professor Spurrier said there may still be other cases, and reminded people who may have been at an exposure site to consider whether they have been previously vaccinated.

Two doses of a measles-containing vaccine are considered effective at preventing illness.

Additional boost may be needed

Professor Spurrier said measles had been increasing in countries that had previously eradicated the disease, including the US, UK and Canada.

She also warned some people may require an additional dose to boost their immunity against the disease.

Measles is a highly contagious infection that can cause severe complications. (Supplied: WA Health)

"[People born] from 1966 onwards may have only had one dose up until being born in the late 1980s," she said.

"If you're not sure, it is not harmful at all to have another dose."

The disease presents with a fever, cough, runny nose and sore eyes initially and usually progresses to a rash.

Serious complications that may require hospitalisation include pneumonia, ear infection and brain inflammation. Extreme cases can cause death.

SA Health advises people who suspect they have measles to phone their doctor before any visit.

The school's principal Rhoni McFarlane said she was appreciative of a temporary vaccination service for the school community.

"It's always concerning when the health and welfare of our community is at stake so our message is to follow health instructions and get immunised if you have not yet been," she said.

title: 'Cynical' Freo coach bemoans how long AFL took with Neale reprieve
text:
Brisbane coach Chris Fagan doubted Lachie Neale would be cleared for the AFL grand final, as his "cynical" Fremantle counterpart Justin Longmuir took umbrage with the lengthy process.

But both coaches are happy with the end outcome, with Fagan declaring Neale's availability "good for footy".

The dual Brownlow Medal winner will feature in the premiership decider against Fremantle — his former club — at the MCG on Saturday after having a one-game ban for striking Hawthorn's Jack Ginnivan downgraded in a drama-filled hearing on Thursday.

Neale was instead fined $10,000 as the appeals board gave the four-time All Australian midfielder the ultimate reprieve due to having never previously been suspended in his decorated 320-game AFL career.

"I didn't think he would (get off)," Fagan told reporters on Friday.

"It was a bit like last year, I didn't think he was going to play last year until the day before the game when he got through a fitness test.

"So it's sort of history repeating itself, just in a different way. Good for footy I reckon but we were pretty much ready for him not to be playing, I must admit."

Brisbane swayed the appeals board that the tribunal had made an error of law in not considering the exceptional and compelling circumstances of Neale's past record.

Longmuir expected Neale to be cleared all along, although thought the decision would have come earlier in the week.

"I'm a bit cynical with these things. Sometimes I feel like that's the outcome that gets reached a little bit later than what I thought it would get reached," the Dockers coach said.

"We prepared for Brisbane's best and he's clearly in their best team. Even if he didn't play, we felt like someone else would have had to step up and they've got a lot of those 'someone else's' that are probably searching for midfield time."

Longmuir later added: "If players who have great records, who have contributed so much to our game, get a bit of leeway at certain times, I don't think that's a bad thing for the game".

Defender Noah Answerth, injured in Brisbane's qualifying final loss three weeks ago, was available and would have returned had Neale been suspended, but misses out.

"Coaches aren't supposed to have favourite players but he's (Answerth) one of mine," Fagan said.

The AFL's gut feel to Neale's gut punch leaves fans dazed and confused It was the AFL's Folarin Balogun moment, and the decision to let Lachie Neale play in the grand final has left many seeing red.

"If Lachie hadn't have played, Noah would have come into the team and Jaspa Fletcher would have pushed up onto a wing."

For the second year in a row, Neale has been the headline story of grand final week.

Last year, the 33-year-old famously overcame a calf injury that appeared season-ending to play a second-half super-sub role in the Lions' stunning demolition of Geelong.

Neale's fourth-straight grand final will almost certainly be his last for Brisbane, with a move to Collingwood looming in the off-season.

"Who says it's my last?" Neale replied to a question about his future.

With rain expected on Saturday, Neale will figure prominently as one of the Lions' best wet-weather players.

Brisbane take an unchanged team into the grand final as they attempt to become just the third side in the last 69 years to complete an AFL premiership three-peat.

And should they win, it would be the second three-peat in their history, following 2001-2003, and it would see them join Melbourne (1939-41 and 1955-57) as one of the only two teams to record the feat twice.

title: Fagan's future undecided as Lions focus on making grand final history
text:
Chris Fagan will again wait until after the grand final to confirm his future as he stands poised to join one of AFL coaching's most select clubs.

There has been speculation over the last few days about whether Saturday could be it for the two-time Brisbane premiership coach.

While Fagan said nothing had changed from the last couple of years — he will speak with Lions hierarchy once the season is over — the 65-year-old acknowledged on Friday that he had been in the role for a decade.

If Brisbane beats Fremantle on Saturday at the MCG, Fagan will become only the seventh VFL/AFL coach to mastermind a premiership three-peat.

"I'm only worried about the game tomorrow," Fagan said at the pre-game media conference.

"Every year, for the last two or three years, I've had a chat with our CEO and president about when's the right time for me to finish up.

"This is my 10th year, so I've been going for a while. I will get through this game and probably have the usual chat I've had every other year."

Chris Fagan has led the Lions to four straight grand finals. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Fagan's long-time confidant Leigh Matthews, who coached the Lions to their 2001-03 three-peat, and former Brisbane captain Jonathan Brown discussed Fagan's future earlier this week.

Brown suspected Fagan would want to try for four in a row if the Lions won. While Matthews said coaching was a lifestyle and Fagan might decide at some point he did not want to do it anymore.

"It's fair enough to speculate about it, but I honestly don't know right at this point in time whether I will keep going or not," Fagan said.

"I was like that last year and the year before, so we just have to work out the right time to go.

"It's not the big issue; we have to play a big game tomorrow."

Justin Longmuir says he is hoping to emulate Chris Fagan's long-term success. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

As Fagan and the Lions try to win another premiership, Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir and his team are looking to win the club's first flag.

Sitting next to Fagan, Longmuir said the goal was to make sure that whatever happened on Saturday, it was only the start of a successful Dockers era.

"I've thought about this moment for a number of years," Longmuir said about the prospect of Fremantle winning the premiership.

"It would fill me with great pride to be able to do that. But win or lose tomorrow, it's not the end of the journey.

"We want to create something that 'Fages' has created, where you're contending for a number of years."

title: Thousands of Queensland child safety workers to walk off the job
text:
Thousands of Queensland child safety workers are set to walk off the job this afternoon over stalled negotiations on pay and conditions.

The Together Union has been negotiating with the state government on a new child safety and youth justice agreement since March and has been taking protected industrial action since August.

The union's assistant secretary, Dee Spink, said members would escalate action on Friday afternoon.

"Our members absolutely don't want to be walking off the job," she said.

"They already donate thousands of hours each month to working for this department and not getting paid for it, but they've simply got no choice in the matter because the government's not taking this seriously."

Together Union assistant secretary Dee Spink. (ABC News)

Child safety workers routinely report caseloads of 30 or more children against an agreed safe caseload of around 16, the union said.

Lucy Besnard, a child safety worker, said it meant kids were not getting their needs met.

"We really try and make sure that every child and young person is safe, but we know that if we can't get to go and do all the visits that we need to do … we know that we're just not doing a good job by them," the union member said.

"We want to, but we just can't."

Lucy Bensard says workers try and make sure that every child and young person is safe (ABC News)

More than 100 child safety officer positions also remain vacant, the union said.

Ms Besnard said the sector has been asked to do more with less and that they have "just run out of less".

She said many members were "sacrificing" being a parent to their own child to ensure children in the system were safe.

Child safety and youth Justice workers across Queensland will walk off the job for about two-and-a-half hours.

Employees are set to bring air mattresses to local members of parliament's offices to highlight cases in which children have spent the night in government offices waiting for suitable placement to be found.

In June, the state government confirmed children in state care have slept in offices but said it is a "rare occurrence".

Premier confirms children have slept in government offices David Crisafulli was briefed after the Together Union acknowledged over the weekend it was aware of reports of children sleeping in child safety offices.

"It's something that shouldn't happen," Ms Besnard said.

A Child Safety Department spokesperson said the government has made an offer and is continuing to negotiate enterprise bargaining agreements in good faith.

"The department has long established business continuity plans in place," the spokesperson said in a statement.

"We will continue to prioritise the safety and wellbeing of children and young people and work to minimise the impact on the delivery of critical services during the work stoppage."

Labor opposition spokesperson Meaghan Scanlon said the child safety system was in crisis and was hurting the state's "most vulnerable".

title: Standing room only as AFL grand final parade kicks off
text:
The threat of rain did little to deter footy fans from swarming Melbourne Park, as the AFL grand final parade rolled past the MCG.

There was a festive atmosphere as Brisbane and Fremantle players smiled and waved at thousands of fans gathered during the parade.

It was standing room only as the AFL Grand Final parade rolled past. ( )

Lions captain Lachie Neale was slightly less animated during the procession, giving brief waves as a smattering of boos could be heard as he drove past.

Lachie Neale was reserved during the Grand Final parade. ( ) Lachie Neale was reserved during the grand final parade. (ABC News: Keira Proust) Kai Lohmann was all smiles during the parade, while Lions legend Alistair Lynch looked less pleased. ( ) Kai Lohmann was all smiles during the parade, while Lions legend Alistair Lynch looked less pleased. (ABC News: Keira Proust) Experienced campaigner Chris Fagan will hope a secure a three-peat tomorrow. ( ) Experienced campaigner Chris Fagan will hope to secure a three-peat tomorrow. (ABC News: Keira Proust)

Neale received a last minute reprieve from the AFL Appeal Board last night, allowing him to play against his old side in his fifth grand final tomorrow.

But Lions fans were out in force to show their team love and drown out the boos, with some admitting there was a sense of déjà vu to proceedings.

Brisbane will play in its fourth grand final in as many years, hoping to replicate its success of the early 2000s with another three-peat.

Lions fan Adele McNamara travelled from Warrnambool for the parade, with a beautiful sign in tow. ( )

In contrast, Fremantle is still searching for its first flag, having lost its only grand final appearance in 2013.

Freo captain Alex Pearce was soaking in the adulation from fans during the parade, as the veteran defender gets ready to play in his first ever grand final.

"It's been great seeing so many Freo fans that have turned up, it doesn't surprise us, they've been with us all year," Pearce said.

"I've got to know them over the 13 years I've been at this club, they're the most passionate fans in the league."

Alex Pearce and John Longmuir were all smiles at the Grand Final parade. ( ) Alex Pearce and John Longmuir were all smiles at the grand final parade. (ABC News: Keira Proust) Luke Jackson will return to the Grand Final after winning the 2021 premiership in Perth. ( ) Luke Jackson will return to the grand final after winning the 2021 premiership in Perth. (ABC News: Keira Proust) Andy Brayshaw and Caleb Serong will play in their first Grand Final tomorrow. ( ) Tens of thousands are expected at Flemington Racecourse this year. (ABC News: Keira Proust)

Despite some more than 3,000km of distance, there was no shortage of Fremantle fans at Melbourne Park.

Many fans said they had flown in from WA during the week, hoping for the chance to glimpse a history-making win.

Fremantle fans turned up in force at Melbourne Park. ( )

It wouldn't be the sacred last weekend in September without an appearance from Mike Brady, who had the crowd laughing before performing his customary rousing rendition of Up There Cazaly.

"You'll know this song ... I call it my superannuation," he said.

There was some extra entertainment for younger fans too, as The Wiggles took to the stage to perform.

Some Lions fans looked sceptical about the allegiances of one particular Wiggle. ( ) Some Lions fans looked sceptical about the allegiances of one particular Wiggle. (ABC News: Keira Proust) Captains Alex Pearce and Josh Dunkley raised the cup to cheers. ( ) Captains Alex Pearce and Josh Dunkley raised the cup to cheers. (ABC News: Keira Proust) Some footballs were looking lost during the parade. ( ) Some footballs were looking lost during the parade. (ABC News: Keira Proust}

Interstate fans flock to Melbourne for big game

For some Lions fans, the AFL grand final parade has simply become an expected yearly pilgrimage.

Tomorrow, the Hall family will be attending their fourth grand final in a row.

Hayley, Henry, Abigail, William and Violet Hall all travelled down from the Sunshine Coast in the hopes of witnessing a premiership three-peat.

"We were here in 2023 when they lost to Collingwood, but we all believe that we wouldn't be going for our three-peat if we didn't lose that one," Hayley Hall said.

"You hope that you're always here the next year, but you just never know, so you just have to savour it as much as you can because you never know when you're gonna be back."

The Hall family has made a habit of heading to the MCG at the end of every September. ( )

But for the youngest member of the Hall clan, grand final day has simply become the norm.

"She's five and she's been at four grand finals, so she's been living a very good life," Ms Hall said.

" She doesn't really know any different apart from the Lions winning. She's living the dream that one. "

In contrast, Lions fans Delaney Biglin and Kyle Moore will be attending their first ever grand final tomorrow, having finally secured tickets.

They said the nerves were beginning to build, but were looking forward to seeing history be made regardless.

"A bit nervous. We're either gonna see a three-peat or we're gonna see Freo's first granny, so it's gonna be great either way," Kyle said.

Kyle Moore and Delaney Biglin were ready for their first ever grand final. ( )

Freo fans Lee Lennon and Jo Crocos flew in from Perth this week, hoping to see their Dockers win their first flag in person.

"We booked in April and paid," Jo said.

"Very confident we were," Lee adds.

"And of course our flights were half-price, weren't they Jo, back in April."

While it was Lee's first time at grand final festivities, Jo was returning after 13 years, having watched Fremantle go down to Hawthorn in the 2013 grand final.

Lee Lennon and Jo Crocos were so confident they'd make the grand final, they book the tickets five months ago. ( )

The pair admitted they were nervous about the game tomorrow, but also quietly confident they could finally snatch the premiership from the Lions.

"I think really it's about time they had another loss so I think it's going to be to us," Lee said.

Sharon Isle and her son Jarvis have also been waiting a long time to see the Dockers win a flag.

Sharon Isle and Jarvis Mill Isle are ready to see the Dockers finally get over the hump and win a grand final. ( )

Jarvis was just seven-years-old when Freo lost its last grand final, and is ready for the club to finally break through.

"I'm hyped. I've been waiting you know 13 years, waiting another seven before that," Jarvis said.

" It's just been incredible to see the boys come this far and the entire country get behind them, not just people from Fremantle. "

"We're flying back home on Sunday ... hopefully with our shirt saying AFL Premiers 2026," Sharon adds.

Grand final first-timers raring to go

For some players on both teams, it was the first time they have experienced the hype and hubbub of grand final weekend festivities.

Ruckman Sam Draper, who made the move to Brisbane this year in the hopes of playing in a grand final, said he was shocked coming out of his hotel this morning and seeing how many fans had gathered.

"It's pretty crazy seeing all the cameras and microphones in front me right now. It's a pretty big deal," Draper said.

"It's been really great having an experienced group. They've told me to just enjoy the week and just embrace it really. Charlie Cameron's been great, he likes to let me know how many grand finals he's played in."

Sam Draper will play in a grand final in his first year with Brisbane. ( )

Oscar Allen will also pull on the guernsey tomorrow and play in his first grand final, after missing out as an emergency in West Coast's 2018 win.

He says things have changed since then.

"To be honest, I was 19-years-old [then] and my head was probably spinning," Allen said.

"A lot of the guys that I played with back then have reached out this week ... I'm just really looking forward to tomorrow afternoon."

Oscar Allen will play in tomorrow's grand final after missing out eight years ago. ( )

"But it's probably more the families and partners. It's very stressful for them trying to sort everything out and I can't speak highly enough of how well the club's done in supporting them and making it a really smooth and easy process for us players so we can just focus on tomorrow afternoon."

Freo forward Jye Amiss said the thought of winning the club's first ever premiership in front of 100,000 people at the MCG had crossed all the players' minds.

"Yeah obviously those thoughts come into your head, you're not human if they don't," Amiss said.

"Obviously it would be awesome for our fans and our community, but our focus is on Saturday and getting the job done."

Jye Amiss says the playing group is not letting the significance of tomorrow's clash put them off their game. ( )

The Dockers have also selected 22-year-old Neil Erasmus for the grand final squad, with the young midfielder saying the magnitude of the occasion hasn't quite sunk in.

"Even just driving in here, seeing all the crowd felt like we were driving to the game almost but we've been pretty settled and it's been a bit of a normal away trip," he said.

"I think tomorrow the nerves will come.

"A lot of us haven't been here before, so it's a first, but the coach has done a really good job of sort of making it feel like a normal week."

title: Australians urged to get free flu jab as season peaks later than usual
text:
Spring has sprung but influenza cases are now only reaching their peak in Australia during a longer flu season than usual.

In the two weeks to September 6, the Australian Respiratory Surveillance report recorded more than 31,000 influenza cases, which is a 27.2 per cent increase from the previous period.

According to the National Notifiable Disease Surveillance Dashboard, there have been 171,440 laboratory-confirmed cases of influenza this year to date

This year, there have been 2,896 confirmed cases recorded in the ACT, 79,376 in NSW, 1,032 in the NT, 33,466 in Queensland, 7,757 in South Australia, 1,672 in Tasmania, 34,552 in Victoria, and 10,689 in Western Australia.

Cases are significantly less than last year but with the season having not yet reached its peak, infectious diseases experts say it is not too late to get vaccinated.

Why is flu season so late this year?

There were several factors contributing to the timing of flu season, University of Queensland virologist Kirsty Short said.

"Some of which are environmental, the circulating strain and the immunity in the population," Professor Short said.

"But what I will say is that this seems to be more going back to what we're used to.

"In so far as after COVID, we saw a shift in flu seasonality where our flu peak came earlier and this sort of represents more what we saw pre-COVID with a bit of a later flu peak."

Hospitals buckle under flu A surge in flu cases puts major pressure on a regional health service on the NSW-Victoria border.

She said it also might be possible people got vaccinated earlier in the year so immunity had waned.

"It's certainly not that immunity completely goes but it does wane over the season and at the start of each season we don't know when the peak will be," she said.

"So it's a really tricky balance to find between the optimal time to get vaccinated, to protect you, but also to ensure longevity of immunity."

Monash University Infectious Diseases expert Allen Cheng said it was a "really strange season".

"Until early to mid-August there had been much less influenza than usual," he said.

"Since the [COVID-19] pandemic, flu epidemiology has been pretty unpredictable so in 2022 it started really early and 2023 also a little bit early."

It is a particular strain of flu?

The most common strain of flu that is circulating is the Super-K subclade of the H3N2 sub-type of Influenza A, Professor Cheng said.

The Super-K flu was the reason for a surge of cases in 2025, which was a record-breaking season.

"I do wonder whether there's something about strain K that is just sort of meant that it's more adapted to spreading it this time of year rather than earlier in the normal time of year," Professor Cheng said.

"One theory is that people thought they got it last year, they might not get it this year but we don't know a lot about flu, particularly the role climate change and humidity play."

Should I still get vaccinated?

Professor Cheng and Dr Short said it was still recommended for people to get vaccinated.

"In previous years I would have said at this time of year if you haven't been vaccinated yet I'd say then you are probably not going to be at risk," Professor Cheng said.

"But this year, because the season is still going and with our experience last year, there is still some benefit."

The federal health department recommends Australians aged six months or older receive an annual flu vaccination and discuss this with their doctor.

Australians at higher risk are eligible for free vaccines under the National Immunisation Program.

title: What scares 'Argentina's Mary Shelley'? Australian suburbia at night
text:
It takes quite a lot to frighten the queen of Latin American gothic horror.

Yet one night as Mariana Enriquez left her local cinema for the short walk home, she was terrified.

She had made the move to Launceston from Buenos Aires only a few months earlier and was struggling to get used to the darkness of Australian suburbia at night.

It also didn't help she had just seen the Australian horror film, Bring Her Back.

"This had never happened to me in my life," she told ABC News.

"I'm almost never scared of horror movies but I was … super terrified when it ended.

"Usually I walk back and that day I was so terrified, I walked one block, got out of the CBD [and there was] darkness ... I called an Uber and told the guy ... 'I have a problem with my leg'."

Mariana Enriquez is considered the queen of Latin American horror by literary critics and book reviewers. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

In her Argentinian home city, darkness meant danger.

It was a hard lesson to unlearn at the age of 50, even in the quietude of northern Tasmania.

"It is one of the biggest [culture shocks] because it's a very everyday thing. If there's a street where you don't have streetlights [in Argentina], it's because it's dangerous, it's abandoned. You don't go there," she said.

"It's a lot of adjusting from being alert always … waiting for something that can come, not just from being unsafe but from other kinds of unsafeness.

" In Argentina you are always… [watching] the news to see if there was some kind of economical disaster that is going to make you make decisions. "

It was the economic precariousness of Argentina which eventually led to Enriquez and her husband moving to Australia around a year ago.

Mariana Enriquez says her subjectivity was shaped by the dictatorship and its aftermath. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

The change has meant she no longer has a relationship with "the immediacy of catastrophe".

"So it's a real reset for me," she said.

In the shadow of a dictatorship

Nicknamed the "Argentinian Mary Shelley", Enriquez has had three collections of short stories and a novel translated into English, in addition to her non-fiction cemetery travelogue, Someone Is Walking On Your Grave.

Enriquez was around two years old when Argentina entered its "big dictatorship" years in 1976, as she calls the country's seven years of military rule which saw the disappearance of around 30,000 people.

During Argentina's seven-year military dictatorship, known as the Dirty War, tens of thousands of people were "disappeared". (Getty images: Horacio Villalobos)

While democracy was eventually restored in 1983, the dictatorship cast a long shadow, even over those who were children at the time.

Enriquez recalled the micro levels of control over everyday life, dictating birthday parties and the number of people who came to your house.

Then there were the years where the full scale of the atrocities were broadcast, a time Enriquez says was in some ways "even more horrifying" than the years of military rule.

Children were not spared from the horror and the "gore" of this very public reckoning.

Photos of young people who were "disappeared" during Argentina's military dictatorship between 1976 and 1983. (Getty: Mondadori Portfolio )

" My subjectivity was formed in that period … Your whole imagination is shaped by this very dark, political thing … There's an alert and an alarm that has to do with growing up like that. "

From a young age, Enriquez had aspirations to be a writer, a resolve that was only strengthened by the discovery such a profession could get you disappeared to one of the more than 500 clandestine prisons dotted around the country.

Argentine horror writer Mariana Enriquez at the grave of French poet Arthur Rimbaud, who was a huge influence on her work. (Supplied: Mariana Enriquez)

"Living through that period and getting out of that period gives people an attitude of never falling for that fear again and fighting back. It was 'They're never going to stop me. They're never going to silence me'."

Enriquez is considered a leading voice in the New Argentine Narrative, a contemporary movement of predominantly women writers whose dark stories confront a collective past.

But in the early days of her writing, Enriquez had some trepidation about how some Argentines would react to her drawing inspiration from that very recent history.

"I was a bit anxious .. if they were going to understand that this was my language as a fiction writer and my way … of taking these issues that were very serious and important to me and very important to the history of our nation and talk about them," she said.

Instead, they embraced her stories.

Three collections of short stories by Mariana Enriquez: The Dangers of Smoking in Bed, A Sunny Place for Shady People and Things We Lost in the Fire. (Supplied)

Alex Cothren, a lecturer in creative writing at Flinders University in Adelaide, who recently hosted Enriquez as a writer in residence, believed the creative lens of horror writing helped Argentines tackle "real deep traumas".

"It's not just the dictatorship; it's the constant crises. They've had [at least] three huge financial crises. Every time the country takes one step forward, it takes two steps back," he said.

"It's a generation of creatives that are trying to tackle these things but they don't want to do that through realism because people are living through it every day.

" So they're doing it through the creative lens of horror which they all grew up from. "

A 'genuine superstar' in Latin America

During Enriquez's residency at Flinders University last month, she had given just one public talk. The ticketed event quickly amassed a waiting list, something Mr Cothren attributed to news of her visit reaching Adelaide's Latin American community.

Mariana Enriquez will appear at the Brisbane Writers' Festival in October. (ABC News: Morgan Timms)

"She's a genuine superstar in Latin America," Mr Cothren said.

"She's now a very big name in our literary culture too. She sells out everywhere she goes."

With so much of her work translated into English, Mr Cothren said Enriquez's work has "exploded" in Australia and other countries.

"She is an expert at creating horror that is not just trying to shock you; it is actually saying something deeper about the place that it comes from," he said.

"There is a real desire for horror that clearly has its roots in something real. It's not enough to just have cool tropes. There is a real urge for depth.

"I know a lot of our young women who are writers really identify with what she writes about."

Mariana Enriquez's novel Our Share of Night (translated into English in 2023) and her non-fiction cemetery travelogue Someone Is Walking On Your Grave (translated into English in 2025). (Supplied)

For her part, Enriquez admits she is still mystified how readers could resonate with her stories, even with one of them, My Sad Dead, forming the basis of a new Netflix series which is due out this week.

"What I do is very personal and very dark. I always find it very weird when people relate to it," she said.

"But I guess young women are now in a place where there's lots ... of anxieties.

" [And] horror speaks perfectly to anxious times ... This era that we're living through, it's an era of anxiety. "

Mariana Enriquez will appear at the Brisbane Writers' Festival in October.

My Sad Dead premieres on September 24 on Netflix.

title: Cowboys blueprint offers NRL expansion hope for Queensland Heartland
text:
The man who turned around the fortunes of the North Queensland Cowboys in the early 2000s believes the campaign officially called the Queensland Heartland Bid is a compelling proposition to become the National Rugby League's [NRL] next expansion club.

The joint Toowoomba and Rockhampton bid, announced this week, extends through the Darling Downs and south-west Queensland and up into central Queensland.

The heartland push would go up against rival bids out of Ipswich and New Zealand.

The Perth Bears will enter the national competition next year before Papua New Guinea in 2028.

NRL boss Peter V'landys is set to reveal the code's 20th team by Christmas, with the new franchise expected to enter the competition in 2029.

Denis Keeffe says the Queensland heartland bid ticks all the boxes. (ABC Capricornia: Alice Roberts)

Denis Keeffe, the former Cowboys chief executive and inaugural CEO of the Central Queensland NRL bid in 2009, said the region's massive geographical footprint made it an obvious choice for NRL expansion.

"It's the heartland, not just rugby league, but it's the economic heartland of this country," Mr Keeffe said.

"If you just look through the record books as to who's come from there rugby league-wise, and where they went and what they did, it fills a journal."

The previous Central Queensland NRL bid supporters included former players like Jason Hetherington and Gary Larsen. (ABC Capricornia: Scott Rollinson)

Mr Keeffe said much of the blueprint developed for the previous Central Queensland bid remained relevant.

"The business plan has been done, and while things have changed since then, the heartland story doesn't change," he said.

" The grassroots are there, the feeder programs are there, all of the green shoots are still there … they just need to be watered a bit. "

The Queensland State of Origin squad in Rockhampton before this year's series decider. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

'It's only going to get bigger'

Before this year's State of Origin decider in June, the Queensland Maroons visited Rockhampton for their annual fan day.

Queensland captain Cameron Munster used the return home to throw his support behind a Central Queensland NRL team.

"It's been a great nursery for kids that have come through to play NRL and it's only going to get bigger," he said at the time.

Yeppoon's Harry Grant receives a rock star welcome home to central Queensland. (Supplied: Rockhampton Regional Council)

While the NRL is considering a potential 20th licence through regional collaborative proposals such as the heartland bid, the code is also facing competition from the AFL as it expands into traditional rugby league territory.

"There's a gap in the middle of Queensland and, in an offensive way, you have to look at your defence as well," Mr Keeffe said.

"Where you've got a gap is where you invite opposition in."

Regional Queensland has unearthed NRLW stars such as CQ's Tamika Upton. (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Regional breeding ground

From Darren Lockyer and Shane Webcke to Cameron Munster and Harry Grant, the Darling Downs, south-west and CQ regions have been a regional breeding ground for NRL, NRLW, State of Origin and international rugby league talent.

Mark Mason is the man behind the Toowoomba and Rockhampton consortium.

The bid team lead said the enormous talent pool was untapped, with the area home to more than 6,000 junior players.

Former premiership-winning Broncos captain Darren Lockyer (left) grew up in the rural Queensland town of Roma. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Linking with Queensland Cup clubs the Western Clydesdales and CQ Capras, Mr Mason said the response from both regional centres had been exciting.

"The community has really come together and united around the bid and, so that sort of reaction has just been incredible," he said.

" They feel like they're a part of something. "

The Toowoomba and Rockhampton bid unites fans and playing talent from two proud rugby league regions. (Elly Bradfield: ABC Southern Queensland)

Mr Mason acknowledged there would be benefits and challenges with the bid spread across two cities.

"There's a great spirit of cooperation between the working parties and there's a core group from Central Queensland and a core group from the Darling Downs that are working well together," he said.

"No doubt there'll be some difficult and tough conversations as we move forward as well.

"But I think both regions are just super excited to be able to be part of this."

The bid will provide a pathway from grassroots footy to the NRL. (AAP: Dave Hunt, file photo)

Toowoomba magnate and director of the Wagner Corporation, John Wagner, said an NRL team would put the region on the map, and be a good incentive for a stadium to be built in the garden city.

"It would be great to see Toowoomba get its own NRL team and that would ultimately mean that one day we would get a decent stadium here in Toowoomba which we desperately need," Mr Wagner said.

" Everyone wins from these things, accommodation providers, the airport creates more jobs, there's no downside to having our own NRL team. "

The North Queensland blueprint

Now-retired Australian sports administrator Denis Keeffe was instrumental in guiding the North Queensland Cowboys from cellar-dwellers to 2004 preliminary finalists.

He did so with a simple game plan — putting local talent at the centre of the club.

The North Queensland Cowboys have enjoyed success connecting with local talent. (AAP: Scott Radford-Chisholm)

He believed the same approach could work for a new team centred around Toowoomba and Rockhampton.

"The way we fixed [the club] up was we introduced North Queensland kids, young men, into the team," he said.

"We doubled our audience in a matter of 18 months because they wanted to connect to their team.

title: Front-running Freo ready to claim first flag
text:
Football fans unite in glory, but the bonds of fandom are often forged in failure.

It is fair to say that Fremantle fans have suffered more than most since their club's entry to the AFL. It's also fair to say that, as a result, Dockers fans are some of the most passionate and dedicated in the league. It's why something like Wharfie Time is endearing instead of cheesy. The Purple Army is something to believe in.

The Fremantle experience has often been one of struggle. Struggling against the bigger brother in blue and yellow. Struggling against the tyranny of distance in a league based on the other side of the continent. Struggling against the weight of its own history.

The anchor is sometimes less a motif of their moniker and instead a weight tethering their expectations.

But this year everything seems different. This year Fremantle has led from the front, often without looking back.

Even as the pack came for the Dockers, they didn't fold under the pressure. Instead, they buckled down and somehow got better.

"The way to win premierships is to win games of footy, and you win games of footy by winning more moments than the opposition," Fremantle coach Justin Longmuir explained last week.

"So we all know what's on the line, but we've just got to make sure that we give our best at each moment, and the next moment's the most important one."

The Dockers showed a resilience often only attached to the best of teams. It's also one baked into the identity of their side.

Fremantle aren't just stocked with high-draft picks. The Dockers are also filled with players overlooked and discarded by others. Almost half of the side that will run out on Saturday fits into those categories, with a few rookies to boot. If these players had given up at the first rejection, they wouldn't be in the league.

More pertinently, Fremantle wouldn't be in the big dance without many of these names.

If Fremantle's fandom and side are somewhat unconventional, its success on the field is anything but. Like many successful teams of years' past, they have been built on a solid defensive base, with enough star power to shine through when needed. Like many great teams, they are more than the sum of their parts.

Like many great teams, they play their best footy when it matters most. Last week, Fremantle put together arguably the best quarter of its season to make the grand final.

"We played our best footy in the last quarter when everything was against us … I'm just so proud of everyone," captain Alex Pearce said in the immediate wake of last week's victory.

Thirteen years after their first grand final, the Dockers finally seem primed to break their premiership drought. In their way stands a side featuring the only remaining Fremantle player from that 2013 loss: Lachie Neale.

Strength in defence

Alex Pearce (right) is the lynchpin of a formidable defensive unit for Fremantle. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Often the leaders of a side dictate the identity and style of a side.

Led ably by captain and All-Australian Alex Pearce, Fremantle's backline may not be as star-studded as other defensive units around the league, but it is as sturdy as any. They scramble, hustle and fight through all four quarters. Regularly through the year teams fell away as the Dockers held strong.

The Dockers have had the league's most consistently good defence across all facets of the game. Some backlines drop their heads when the tide starts to turn — not Fremantle.

Fremantle excels at defending before danger begins. Its midfield works hard to prevent clean exits from stoppages and contests around the ground. Although the Dockers don't have the best clearance differential or ability to win ground balls in the mid-arc, they are exceptional at preventing opposition teams from scoring from these sources.

When they lose possession in their front half, the Dockers stay eager to get the ball in their hands. They are the best side in the league at winning the ball back in the middle third of the ground.

If the ball does end up inside their defensive 50, no side is better at repelling opposition forwards. Miserly is an understatement about how Fremantle defends. It is the biggest reason that the Dockers are still alive in season 2026.

When they win the ball back, they can turn on the jets and blow opposition sides away.

The cherry on top

Players such as Luke Jackson (left) and Shai Bolton (right) ensure Fremantle can beat teams offensively as well as defensively. (AAP Image/Richard Wainwright)

Few fans turn up to the footy for stout defence. It's the action at the other end that hypnotises.

Despite their defensive DNA, Freo are not lacking for weapons of their own. They turn defence into attack at the drop of a hat thanks to a plethora of creative players.

Fremantle can put on a show like few others when everything is firing, possessing the ability to pile goal after goal on the scoreboard. While their defence is often understated, their attack is anything but.

Few players generate more highlights than Shai Bolton, with the former Mark of the Year winner routinely getting Purple fans off the edge of their seats. Bolton isn't alone however.

The Dockers side is stocked with players that use the ball well.

Murphy Reid has quickly cemented himself as an attacking line breaker, while Caleb Serong, Jordan Clark and Corey Wagner gain ground with ease.

Luke Jackson also proves a challenge for any opponent as the most capable ruck at ground level in the league. Jackson has the most score involvements of any ruck this year.

The Dockers often attack in straight lines, and use the tallest timber in the league to their advantage.

But when sides like Sydney take those avenues away, Fremantle doesn't shy away from changing angles of attack and look laterally as well.

That ability to win aerial contests has another benefit. It tends to encourage opposition players to fly more often than they should, leaving Fremantle with an outnumber at ground level. That allows even more room for the ground gang to work in.

Up forward, the Dockers can beat you in any number of ways. The likes of Hye Amiss, Patrick Voss and Josh Treacy can take clunks and convert them into sure scores. At ground level, Michael Frederick, Isaiah Dudley and Shai Bolton regularly hit the scoreboard and strike fear into the hearts of opposition small defenders.

Their big men love a bomb from the top of the arc, but Freo don't tend to score a lot from out wide. That makes Hayden Young's preliminary final heroics all the more notable.

Perhaps Fremantle's biggest strength is their evenness across the board. Against Hawthorn it wasn't just the stars like Bolton and Luke Jackson that stood up late, but also players like Judd McVee and Frederick. It is clear that there's belief in this team, and dedication to a united cause.

The Final Challenge

Lachie Neale (centre) and the Brisbane Lions are standing between Fremantle and its maiden premiership. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

Although Fremantle has been the best side across the year, it isn't coming into the grand final at the peak of its mid-season powers. The Dockers have won just three quarters in their three finals so far — a feat no other team has achieved before.

The Dockers have struggled late in the year when the ball has hit the deck against good sides, and some of the best midfields have overwhelmed their attacking midfield unit. These may sound like minor issues, but to win a grand final against the two-time defending champions, everything has to be on point.

But the Lions are a side that the Dockers have vanquished through the year. In round 12, the Dockers eased to a 25-point win in one of their most impressive wins of the year. The Dockers absorbed the Lions' clearance dominance while preventing them from getting the upper hand in the marking battle. Fremantle worked out a way to penetrate the Lions' whole ground defence, scoring a massive 52 points from their defensive half.

But it was also a Brisbane side that Longmuir acknowledged wasn't at their best coming into the game.

Fremantle got the better of Brisbane in the only meeting between the two sides during the home-and-away season this year. (Getty Images: Russell Freeman)

"We felt like there were some opportunities there. You know, Fages [Lions coach Chris Fagan] would come in here and say they're not in the greatest form," he said.

"I just don't want to be disrespectful with that because they've been in the last three grand finals."

Longmuir and Fagan both know that premierships aren't won in May. The early season Lions are vastly different to the side that Fremantle has to beat in the grand final.

But there's hope in the West that the result will be the same and that the Dockers three-decade drought will be over.

title: Viral squishy toy trend putting children in hospital with burns
text:
They are soft, often sparkly, a sensory delight and the current must-have for children around the world.

But what the viral squishy toys are made of is often not disclosed and a social media trend has put dozens of Australian children in hospital with serious burns.

Squishies are squeezable toys usually made from a thermoplastic rubber outer shell and filled with polyvinyl alcohol (PVA), maltose — a sugar-like substance — gels, beads and other materials.

Squishy toys come in all shapes and sizes and are easy to find online and in shops. (ABC News: Liana Walker)

They come in a range of shapes and sizes, from cubes to capybaras, and can be purchased anywhere from large department stores to small pop-up shops and online.

Demand for the toys has driven a rise in counterfeits that often do not disclose their contents, leading one manufacturer to ask the Australian Border Force (ABF) to stop them from entering the country.

Dangerous microwave trend

Even when the toys disclose their make-up and undergo safety testing, however, they are not completely risk-free.

A viral online trend has children microwaving squishies, resulting in serious injuries.

People have been putting squishy toys in the microwave because of a social media trend. (Supplied: Tiktok)

A Sydney Children's Hospitals Network spokesperson said between January and September this year, 11 children were referred to the Burns and Plastics Treatment Centre at the children's hospital at Westmead for burns caused by heated squishy toys.

"Children were aged between 6 and 12 years old with burns ranging from mid to deep burns on the face, neck, chest, arms and hands," the spokesperson said.

"Some children sustained burns that required skin grafts and longer-term scar treatment."

Queensland Children's Hospital paediatric emergency physician Veevek Thankey said that, since April, he was aware of at least 13 burn cases linked to squishy toys being heated.

"The biggest issue that we've seen is actually the burns themselves as opposed to the actual reactions to the content that's present within these toys," he said.

Veevek Thankey is aware of at least 13 burn cases linked to squishy toys. (Supplied: Children's Health Queensland)

Dr Thankey said most of the issues have been with burns to the hands or face, which require "intensive management".

He said that because the gel liquid becomes sticky, burns can occur extremely fast.

If an incident occurs, Dr Thankey said the most effective first aid was to remove any of the gel from the skin and place the affected burn area under cool running water for 20 minutes.

A Tasmanian Department of Health spokesperson confirmed its burns unit was aware of a small number of injuries caused by these toys.

Other health jurisdictions were unable to confirm if there were any reports of injuries related to the toys.

Do you know more? Contact Liana Walker at walker.liana@abc.net.au

Counterfeit concerns

NeeDoh manufacturer Schylling has asked the ABF for help to stop counterfeits. (Reuters: Erin Jones-USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)

The sudden popularity of the toys has led to a boom in counterfeits.

It is something Schylling, the manufacturer behind NeeDoh, has taken extremely seriously, asking the ABF to seize counterfeit products entering the country.

William Valentine, the distributor of NeeDoh in Australia, confirmed it had taken steps to combat counterfeit products, including registering its intellectual property with the ABF Notice of Objection scheme.

"Counterfeit products don't just infringe on our intellectual property — they bypass the rigorous design, manufacturing, quality control and independent safety testing that authentic NeeDoh products undergo before reaching consumers," managing director Benjamin Halls said.

"That's why we take the growing issue of counterfeit toys so seriously."

Needoh Nice Cube lists its ingredients as 100 per cent malt extract. (ABC News: Liana Walker)

Mr Valentine said the company was also working with local counsel to identify sellers of counterfeit products and take appropriate legal action.

Consumer watchdog the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) confirmed it has been liaising with several domestic and international regulators in relation to squishy toys, along with online marketplaces and businesses.

It said there were mandatory standards regarding the levels of lead and other chemicals contained in products, and warned of consequences if businesses fail to comply.

Counterfeits seized globally

The Isle of Man's government seized numerous counterfeit squishy toys being sold. (Supplied: Isle of Man Government )

In the UK, the Office for Product Safety and Standards issued a recall for Samsons Cash and Carry Squeezy Dumplings after they were found to contain an excess concentration of benzene — a chemical linked to leukaemia.

Thousands of toys, including squishy toys, were seized in shops across north-east Lincolnshire. Another 81 were seized from a retailer on the Isle of Man.

In the US, the Consumer Product Safety Commission has also issued a warning about counterfeit squishy toys, with 55 shipments of noncompliant squishy toys stopped at US ports, preventing more than 355,000 units from entering the country.

Squishy bun toys containing water beads were seized in the US. (Supplied: The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission)

A professor of analytical chemistry at RMIT, Oliver Jones, said that while the unknown chemical make-up of squishy toys can be concerning, they were most likely made from the same materials.

"It's just that the manufacturing quality and the amounts [of chemicals] that might be left over in the final product could be worse if you've got one of these counterfeit ones that have been made at short notice without proper oversight and brought onto the market here," he said.

Dr Jones said other qualities, such as the thickness of the material on the outside of the toy and its robustness, were also concerns for knock-offs.

The ACCC recommended consumers avoid toys with strong chemical smells, weak seams, loose beads and leaking parts and to look for clear safety information, including ingredient or material information.

Some squishy toys do not include ingredients lists or safety information. (ABC News: Liana Walker)

However, Dr Jones said most of these toys were made at a quality standard.

"If you bought it from a reputable shop … and it doesn't smell and it's got listing of what's in it and so forth, I wouldn't be particularly worried as long as it's used in the way it's intended," he said.

"Even if it's like the best quality made toy in the world, if you put it in the microwave, that's an extra risk.

"And I'd certainly be a bit careful about leaving them in hot cars, just to be on the safe side.

"We just have to be careful that when something does go wrong, then we learn from it. And if we can improve safety with better data on what's in the toy and how it's been manufactured, that can't be a bad thing."

title: Retiring Dolphin lauded as one of NRL's toughest ahead of prelim final
text:
Ray Stone has claims to being the toughest man in the NRL.

Not that the Dolphins' warrior would care two hoots for the title as he nears retirement at the end of the 2026 season at the tender age of 29.

But there was a reason coach Kristian Woolf singled him out at last year's presentation night for playing the last six rounds with a broken hand and final 15 rounds with needles in both shoulders.

He had off-season shoulder surgery after pushing himself to play when the Dolphins had multiple forwards on the injured list.

Stone is one of those players who performs when busted. When fit and relatively injury-free, though, he is even more dangerous.

"There are a lot of tough men who play our game but he is in the top group," Woolf said.

"It is not just his toughness, it's his commitment to the team that I really admire.

"He is just a guy who refuses to let his teammates down. It doesn't matter if it is playing injured, he is making an effort on a kick-chase, getting into a tackle or a carry.

"I love his hit-ups off the kick-off. I get a kick out of watching those because he runs so hard. He is just committed to the team. That is what we are going to miss."

Stone has been linked to a boxing career but AAP understands he has obtained multiple tickets in trade areas and will only get in a ring if he sees fit. He can hold them up, as the saying goes.

Finals battle between an unstoppable force and an immovable object Brian To'o and Greg Marzhew have never met a rugby league problem they couldn't solve by running over it and now the two wrecking balls will go head-to-head with an NRL grand final berth on the line.

"It is probably based on family time for me," Stone said, when asked why he was calling time.

"The kids are getting a bit older and I am quite busy on weekends so I want to be a part of that."

Woolf wanted him on deck in 2027.

"I have spoken to him a number of times and asked if I could change his mind but he has got other things in life he wants to do," the coach said.

"I respect that about him. He knows what he wants. He has pushed himself through the pain."

Stone was the second player signed at the Dolphins after starting his NRL career at Parramatta, where he played 31 matches in five seasons. At the Dolphins, he has notched 81 games in four years.

Dolphins coach Kristian Woolf has tried his very best to convince Stone to play on next season.

"The reason I came up here was for opportunity," he said.

"I was in and out of first-grade at Parramatta where we had a strong team and I spoke to Wayne Bennett about coming here and he said I'd be more of a consistent first-grader."

The warhorse, who plays mostly off the bench, has scored eight tries for the Dolphins but, like an old-school footy player of the past, he doesn't smile after any.

"It's not something I stress about," Stone said, through gritted teeth.

"I like to leave all my celebrating until after the game when the boys have got the result."

The Dolphins have won 16 of their last 18 matches coming into Friday night's NRL preliminary final. (Getty Images: Matt King)

He's done plenty of that this year, with the Dolphins winning 16 of their last 18 matches ahead of the preliminary final against Sydney Roosters.

"This year I've been a lot healthier and the squad has too, which has definitely helped our middle rotation," Stone said.

"Last year, pretty much our whole starting pack was in rehab. The minutes have been distributed a lot more which has helped me stay healthy."

Woolf is just glad to have Stone in the team after he missed the early rounds with his shoulder recovery.

"We did miss him too. He is a small man in a big man's world who plays so tough," Woolf said.

"He is loved, respected and will be missed next year.

"He is going to leave a legacy that people don't realise. There are no discipline issues around Ray. He turns up and gets his job done every day of every week."

AAP

title: Former AFL star 'shattered' as partner dies two days after giving birth
text:
Former West Coast Eagles player Mark Hutchings says his partner Hannah has died two days after the birth of their daughter.

Hutchings revealed her death in a social media post late yesterday.

"It is with deep sadness that I share the sudden loss of my beautiful partner, Hannah," he wrote on Instagram.

"2 days following the birth of our daughter, Sofia.

"I am shattered."

Loading Instagram content

Hutchings said Hannah had been looking forward to motherhood.

"Her dream was to become a Mum, so it's been incredibly difficult to take," he wrote.

"Sofia and I love you and will miss you very much Hannah."

A one-club player, Hutchings played 120 AFL games for the Eagles, and was part of the 2018 team that won a premiership by defeating Collingwood in the grand final.

A host of AFL players and former West Coast teammates, including Jeremy McGovern, Jack Darling and Mitch Brown, left messages of support in the comment section on the Instagram post.

Mark Hutchings played 120 AFL games for the Eagles and was part of the 2018 premiership-winning team. (AAP: Dave Hunt)

"You'll be the best Dad for your beautiful daughter, we got you," retired ruckman Nic Naitanui said.

"Thinking of you mate. Sending all our love your way," Mark LeCras said.

In his social media post, Hutchings thanked his friends, family, former teammates and colleagues for their sympathy.

"Thank you for all of your messages of support, I can't always reply to them all but I do appreciate them," he wrote.

No further details about Hannah's death were provided.

title: New generation of students carries Tongan culture forward
text:
Si'i Kae Hā, meaning "small but significant" in Tongan, is the name of Robinvale Secondary College's Tongan dance group.

Last week, the group lived up to its name when 24 students travelled eight hours from the small town of Robinvale in Victoria's north-west to perform at the Cultivating Creative Cultures with Communities (4Cs) Showcase in Melbourne.

They were the first regional Victorian group to perform in the showcase in its 20-year history.

Robinvale College captains Ruby Hingano and Sione Heitonga have been part of Si'i Kae Hā since its inception. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

College captains Sione Heitonga and Ruby Hingano helped establish the dance group in 2023 as a way for students to connect with their culture and community.

Ruby, who is both Aboriginal and Tongan, said joining the group has helped her discover a side of her identity she did not grow up knowing.

"Starting this group let me connect with my Tongan side more and with more of my family too," she said.

Si'i Kae Hā performing their 4Cs Showcase set for their school during an assembly. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

Passing culture to the next generation

Robinvale College education support workers Lueni Kolofale and Samuel Fangatua, who have been a driving force behind the group, also grew up in Robinvale.

They were taught by Tongan elders who helped keep their culture alive.

Their school experience was filled with regular opportunities to perform at annual showcases, community events and travelling roadshows.

Robinvale College staff who have helped bring Si'i Kae Hā to life. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

When Ms Kolofale and Mr Fangatua returned as staff, many of those opportunities were gone.

The pair saw an opportunity to rebuild that connection, helping to pass cultural knowledge on to another generation.

Si'i Kae Hā girls dancing during the Robinvale College assembly. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

Mr Fangatua said the Si'i Kae Ha group had grown beyond just dance, with students' curiosity branching out to Tongan traditions, culture and language.

He said that connection had flowed into their education.

"They're not going to do well in their education if they don't know who they are," he said.

Students are expected to maintain their behaviour and schoolwork to take part in performances and trips.

Ms Kolofale said students had gradually learnt that representing their culture also meant living its values of respect and love.

One parent, Sela Tuiaki Ale, said she had seen that change in her own children.

Sela Tuiaki-Ale with her son Latu Masila and daughter Suliana Mafi. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

Her children were raised speaking English, as she and her partner were also born and raised in Australia.

She said the dance group had given them another way to learn about their Tongan heritage.

"They were born and raised here, so to see them still want to learn about our culture and live in it as well is really good," she said.

Her parents and grandparents had embraced the opportunity too, helping dress the students in traditional attire and watching them perform.

Ms Ale's family was one of many who had played a role in the group's success.

Tongan elder Lupe Taumoefolau helping the students prepare to perform. (ABC News: Lua Ikenasio)

A community effort

In the lead-up to the 4Cs showcase, the community raised $10,000 to take the students to Melbourne.

Parents and Tongan elders helped create the traditional wear and teach the dances.

The significance of the journey was not lost on 4Cs director Latini Matautia-Ulugia.

"It really does take a lot of people to okay something like this," she said.

"The fact that the school said yes and gave them the opportunity to fundraise and then were supported by community, I thought that was really is something that should be shared."

Department of Education Regional Director Tip Kennedy attended to support the school, the first time a department representative had attended the event.

Sione said he was nervous in the lead-up to the night and had "prayed countless times", while Ruby said that despite the nerves, she was just excited to perform.

Si'i Kae Hā boys dancing for their school. (Lua Ikenasio)

Both said that once they hit the stage, they were filled with pride.

For their teachers, watching the students carry their culture onto a Melbourne stage was a moment of awe.

"When we got to the venue in Melbourne we were like … who do we think we are coming all this way, doing all of this? From little Robinvale?" Ms Kolofale said.

The group is already looking forward to returning next year.

For now, Si'i Kae Ha continues to give Robinvale students a way to carry their culture forward, thousands of kilometres from Tonga.

title: Customers say Qantas not being 'fair dinkum' on costly outback flights
text:
For anyone travelling to Queensland's "capital of the outback", a flight could cost more than an interstate or overseas trip.

John Elliott was "staggered" to discover earlier this month that a return flight between Brisbane and Longreach would cost $1,386, even though he booked five days in advance.

The cost of the two-and-a-half-hour flight was equivalent to a last-minute Qantas flight to Auckland and only $450 less than a last-minute budget flight to Singapore.

John Elliott wants airlines to prove that remote flights cost them as much as they say. (ABC Western Qld: Crispian Yeomans)

"I think it stops a lot of people travelling. Basically, the only visitors that we get to western Queensland have to drive," Mr Elliott said.

Mr Elliott, who has formerly coordinated events in Winton, said he had seen expensive rural flights deter not just outback residents, but also potential holiday-makers and those bringing drawcard tourism events to the west.

He said "corporate Australia" was treating people in the bush "with a lack of respect".

"Whenever we had a big event, it was cheaper for us to charter an 80-seater jet and fly direct from Brisbane into Winton [than book a commercial flight]," he said.

"I just don't think Qantas are being fair dinkum at the moment."

Qantas is the only airline that services the route between Longreach and Brisbane.

Outback routes already subsidised

Of the more than 40 routes in regional Queensland, seven servicing 23 towns take airfare subsidies from the state government.

Maximum fares on these regulated routes are capped where demand is considered "too low" to be commercially viable.

Contracts currently held by Rex and Qantas are reviewed every five years, but the Department of Transport and Main Roads has delayed its decision by 12 months so it can "consider all the feedback" from 37 consultation sessions.

The larger Qantas 737 jets have double the number of seats, which can reduce the overall cost per passenger. (ABC Kimberley: Andrew Seabourne)

It's not the only review underway: the Australian Productivity Commission is also inquiring into the cost of regional airfares, with a draft report due in November.

In its submission, Qantas said Dash 8-400 planes were the "most suitable" aircraft to service smaller or remote regional routes because they had "lower maintenance and operating costs" than the smaller Q200 and Q300.

But the carrier said the aircraft, which carried fewer than half the passengers of a standard commercial jet, were not as profitable due to the "economy of scale".

"On average, these services are more than twice as expensive to operate than Qantas 737s and about three times more expensive than Jetstar and Qantas international services on a per-passenger basis," the submission said.

Outback residents face sky-high airfares Outback residents are paying the price of an international ticket to travel to their nearest capital city.

The airline has been contacted for comment.

Central Queensland University aviation expert Steve Leib said the fleet of smaller planes used on rural routes tended to be older and more expensive to operate.

"The costs just continue to creep up as aircraft age … and those smaller aircraft with fewer seats are in less of a position to help you recover the revenue associated with that [maintenance]," Dr Leib said.

Shaun Radnedge is calling for more regional flights and more affordable fares. (Supplied: Murweh Shire )

Calls for airlines to 'justify' prices

Several councils in the south-west have been lobbying for a new contract with the government

Murweh Shire Mayor Shaun Radnedge said prices were not the only issue.

"Every plane is full at the moment. People are saying they can't access seats," he said.

"We have had health services actually had to postpone what they had planned here in Charleville because they could not get a seat."

Cr Radnedge said now the region would be "in limbo" for another year, before they could bring in more flights and more affordable fares.

He said the state government had not consulted with his shire about delaying the review.

John Elliott is concerned costly outback airfares are sending tourists to other towns or overseas. (ABC Western Qld: Maddelin McCosker)

Now living in Toowoomba, Mr Elliott said governments should force carriers to prove whether remote flights really cost them as much as they claimed.

"I think the federal government need to say to Qantas, 'You need to be fair dinkum, you need to be transparent,'" he said.

"You need to justify how you can charge that much for a flight that really doesn't equate to anything their operation does [else]where in Australia."

title: Premiership winner Ah Nee Nwe wants to be first Karen AFL player
text:
Ah Nee Nwe may not be a household name yet, but after starring in the Nhill Tigers under-14s' first grand final win in almost 30 years, that might not be the case for long.

Nwe's junior side in Victoria's far west broke a 28-year drought to defeat Ararat by seven points, with the teenager named best on ground.

Seven years ago, Nwe had barely heard of Australian Rules football, let alone kicked a Sherrin.

But fast forward to the last Saturday in September and he was launching long-range goals and inspiring his teammates as one of nine Karen boys in the drought-breaking side.

Ah Nee Nwe says he loves playing footy with his mates. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

"I'm finding AFL pretty good; it's fun with mates," he said.

The Karen are an ethnic group from Myanmar, many of whom fled conflict and persecution by crossing into Thailand.

At least three boys in the grand final-winning team were born in refugee camps.

Nwe is a first-generation Karen; his mother, Cho Lay, arrived in Nhill 16 years ago.

It did not take him long to fall in love with footy.

The Karen boys helped Nhill break a 28-year premiership drought. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

"It's good — playing and learning new things, having more opportunities in life," he said.

"I wasn't that good [at football], but then I kept training and practising more, and I got better."

He said he dreams of playing professionally one day.

"I would feel very proud of myself as being the first Karen possibly to make it to the AFL," he said.

"If I make the AFL, I bet the club will hold a celebration and the Karen [community will be] all happy … and Nhill will be very proud."

Ah Nee was named best on ground in the grand final. (Supplied: Tania McQueen)

Travelling full circle

According to the 2021 census, Karen people make up around 10 per cent of the Nhill population.

Margaret and John Millington were instrumental in bringing the first Karen refugees to the town in 2010.

Mr Millington was the managing director of Luv-a-Duck, one of the largest duck meat producers in the country, which was struggling to find local workers.

He had never heard of the Karen people, but heard a number of refugees wanted to move to the nearby town of Horsham.

Mr Millington was soon able to hire five Karen workers.

John and Margaret Millington were instrumental in bringing the Karen refugees into Nhill. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

"Five [workers] became six, became 10 and it just grew from there," Mr Millington said.

Ms Millington said the town had since embraced the Karen people, with around 35 businesses across the Wimmera now employing them.

"They brought more than just their skills, more than just their employment," she said.

"We saw on the weekend the success of the under 14s … I think half the under 14s were actually little Karen boys who were vital for the survival of the club."

The grand final win was an emotional moment for Mr Millington.

"I must say, I had a tear in my eye there in the last quarter … it was that exciting," he said.

"It's been a community effort, but to the credit of the community, I think we've seen the success through those kids playing.

Nhill's under-14 side defeated Ararat by seven points in the grand final. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

"After Saturday winning the grand final, people will realise the importance of having them and what a gift they are to our community in so many ways."

Kicking goals

Nhill Football Netball Club's Tracey Bell has been crucial in bringing the Karen families to the club.

She said her own children might have had to move clubs if the Karen community had not helped fill the junior playing ranks.

"It gave those kids an opportunity to be involved in our club and community, when they might have had other challenges — like their parents not speaking English" she said.

Ms Bell said building trust with the Karen families took time and consistency early on.

"I had to work with them, bring them to trainings, communicate with their families through the Karen liaisons at school," she said.

She said she relied on her own children, and on Karen boys with stronger English, to help translate for others in the group.

There are now more than 35 kids involved across football and netball.

Tracey Bell says the Karen community has bolstered player numbers at the club. (ABC News: Nethma Dandeniya)

"We're really proud that our club and the kids, the coaches and our community have really embraced them," she said.

"Seeing all the kids turn up, they come to footy training, they just want to be involved.

"There's no way we would have been able to play or field a 14s team, let alone take out a grand final on Saturday without them.

"Looking at the extended community that attended the grand final, it was unprecedented for an under-14s game … I think it speaks volumes about how much the community supports all of our kids."

title: Enchanting performance propels properly lovely musical revival
text:
Sydney Opera House, September 22

Until October 31



Someone said to me, “Not My Fair Lady again!” But when it’s this good, 10 years seems rather too long between elocution lessons. It still makes most other musicals seem trashy, with their cartoon characters, simplistic stories and limp or overwrought songs.

Nor could Alan Jay Lerner (book and lyrics) and Frederick Loewe (music) ever replicate such mastery. But then, they never again had such robust raw material as George Bernard Shaw’s Pygmalion.

So right for the part: Claire Lyon as Eliza Doolittle in My Fair Lady. Photo Jeff Busby

The pressure on the performers playing Eliza Doolittle and Henry Higgins is frightening given the many brilliant predecessors, beginning with Julie Andrews and Rex Harrison in 1956. Claire Lyon and Nathaniel Parker duly won us anew.

Lyon has wanted to play Eliza all her life, unsuccessfully auditioning for the 2016 incarnation of this production, which, directed by Andrews and produced by John Frost and Opera Australia, was conceived to replicate the original Broadway designs. Now Karen Johnson Mortimer replicates Andrews’ direction.

Lyons performance is a victory for all who don’t give up and a lesson for all directors and producers. She’s 18 years older than Eliza is supposed to be, yet she’s so right for the part that this discrepancy is swept away – other than for allowing her to present an Eliza who’s a little more knowing, a little less the ingenue.

Claire Lyon as Eliza Doolittle Jeff Busby

Lyon blossomed more after the opening scene, blossomed yet more when she mastered “the rain in Spain”, and still more when she tapped into the inner steel to stand up to Higgins’ bullying. All Elizas must own our hearts, and Lyon’s performance enchants as she effortlessly blends comedy, elegance and singing with a beautifully rounded soprano voice.

The trick with playing Higgins is for the actor to charm us into forgiving his tyranny towards Eliza, as he elevates her from a flower girl to gentlewoman, just to win a bet. If that charm is not in place, why does Eliza fall for him, given her treatment?

Parker being two decades older than Higgins’ putative age of 40 creates a fatherly dimension that clouds the phenomenally nuanced frisson of allure between Higgins and Eliza. Nonetheless, he’s splendid at being bumptious, intelligent and emotionally asinine. His delivery of the fizzing lyrics was supreme in You Did it and Hymn to Him, although he undersold some of the delicious lines in I’ve Grown Accustomed to Her Face.

Nathaniel Parker as Professor Henry Higgins. Jeff Busby

Reg Livermore, Tony Llewellyn-Jones and Robyn Nevin reprise their roles as Alfred Doolittle, Colonel Pickering and Mrs Higgins to sterling effect, with Livermore somehow evading the passing years.

The recreations of Oliver Smith’s sets and Cecil Beaton’s costumes are also stars, as are the songs, of course, realised with intricate detail by the orchestra under David Young. The ensemble looks transcendent in the Ascot scene (with choreography by Christopher Gattelli), as the English stiff upper lip migrates to stiff upper bodies. You’d be mad to miss it.
