Zenith Minerals has struck gold in all six of the first holes assayed in a drill campaign designed to bridge a 600-metre gap between two key deposits at its flagship consolidated Dulcie gold project in Western Australia. The initial results from a recently completed program include a notable 3-metre intersection grading 2.48 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 130m, with the promising results hinting at the potential to bridge the gap and link the deposits. A drill rig in action at Zenith Minerals’ Consolidated Dulcie gold project in Western Australia. The drilling targeted the previously untested ‘Dulcie Central’ corridor, a stretch of ground sitting between the company’s Dulcie North and Dulcie deposits. Management says the early success supports its geological theory that the prospective host sequence and the gold-bearing Dulcie shear zone extend continuously through the project’s hefty six-kilometre corridor. Other significant intercepts include 4m at 1.3g/t gold, 6m at 0.93 g/t gold and 2m at 2.42g/t gold.

‘First results confirm gold mineralisation within the gap and support our geological interpretation.’ Zenith Minerals managing director Andrew Smith The drill program is aimed at growing the project’s existing 675,000-ounce gold resource. However, with historical hits at the broader project already delivering stunners such as 32m at 9.4 g/t gold and 3m at 70 g/t gold, any success in proving up a continuous mineralised system could significantly enhance the project’s overall scale and pit economics. Zenith has now completed all holes in the 4601m reverse circulation (RC) program and is awaitingassays from the remaining 25 holes. The company says it expects those results to land sometime in October. Zenith Minerals managing director Andrew Smith said: “Gold mineralisation in all six of the first holes at Dulcie Central is an encouraging start to the programme. This is previously untested ground between the Dulcie North and Dulcie deposits and these first results confirm gold mineralisation within the gap and support our geological interpretation that the prospective host sequence and Dulcie shear extend through Dulcie Central.” The positive results, which appear to be proving up the ground, come as corporate machinations unfold in the background. An off-market scrip takeover by Forrestania Resources to scoop up Zenith and its Dulcie gold project for a reported $93.5 million remains ongoing as the particulars of the takeover are ironed out and its largest shareholders are mollified.

The company’s refocused diamond drilling at the project has now traced gold mineralisation beyond 700 metres vertical depth, reinforcing the continuity of a broad breccia-hosted intrusion-related gold system (IRGS). Once all results are in for Dulcie, management says it will assess whether the drilling warrants a maiden mineral resource estimate for the central corridor tenement and a potential update to the existing resource at the adjacent Dulcie South. While takeover talks continue, Zenith appears focused on the task at hand - systematically testing the ground and adding ounces at Dulcie. Proving up gold mineralisation across the 600-metre gap would be a compelling step forward and with a flood of assays just around the corner, the full picture of what lies between the Dulcie deposits is about to get a whole lot clearer. Kuniko Limited has wrapped up phase two diamond drilling at the company’s Commonwealth-Silica Hill project in New South Wales, completing a five-hole, 1492-metre campaign designed to expand the mineralised system ahead of a resource update. Assay results from the phase two drilling campaign are expected in October. The now-completed program was designed to test and extend the interpreted Northern and Southern lodes at its Silica Hill prospect. Since kicking off its earn-in on the project in October 2025, the company has completed 11 diamond drill holes for a combined 2731m. The expanded dataset will help firm up the mineralised system’s geological interpretation ahead of an updated resource estimate, which the company has slated for the fourth quarter of this year. Kuniko Limited drill rig on site during phase two diamond drilling at its Commonwealth-Silica Hill project in the heart of the rich Lachlan fold belt in NSW. Kuniko’s earn-in and joint venture with Impact Minerals give it the right to secure up to a 90 per cent interest in the project. Currently, its primary deposits at Commonwealth and Silica Hill have JORC-inferred mineral resource estimates totalling 88,000 ounces of gold and 3.3 million ounces of silver. The impetus for Kuniko’s latest campaign came from a spectacular, bonanza-grade hit during the first phase of drilling, which delivered a stunning 0.5-metre intercept grading an eye-watering 20,603 grams per tonne (g/t) silver and 27g/t gold. Phase two has also served up early promise, with visual logging revealing broad zones of sulphides up to 70m wide and individual veins as thick as half a metre.

Advertisement

‘We are advancing a pipeline of regional targets across the broader district-scale system.’ Kuniko Limited managing director Maja McGuire The Commonwealth- Silica Hill project comprises two distinct but related deposits within 200m of each other. The Commonwealth Main and South deposits are a polymetallic volcanogenic massive sulphide style system with high-grade gold, silver and zinc. The nearby Silica Hill deposit is an epithermal stockwork vein system that hosts high-grade silver mineralisation. Kuniko managing director Maja McGuire said: “Completing Phase 2 drilling is an important milestone for Kuniko, with 11 diamond holes now completed for 2,731 metres across the Commonwealth-Silica Hill system. The program has significantly advanced our understanding of the mineralised system, with assays expected in October and planned DHEM surveys to provide further insight into potential extensions.” Commonwealth-Silica Hill sits in the heart of the revered Lachlan Fold Belt, a region widely described by market commentators as a tier-1 copper-gold province and home to some of Australia’s mining giants. The belt, which hosts major operations including Newmont’s goliath 30 million ounce Cadia-Ridgeway mine, is seeing renewed exploration fervour, partly thanks to the ongoing success of ASX-listed Alkane Resources at its nearby Boda-Kaiser porphyry copper-gold deposit. That project now features a hefty resource of more than 8.3 million ounces of gold and 1.5 million tonnes of copper, providing a compelling backdrop for any explorer making headway along the same trend.

Advertisement

The use of geophysics to define new targets and extensions has played a key role in the exploration success at Boda-Kaiser, putting Kuniko’s conductor-focused next move neatly in step with the regional exploration playbook. Selected holes from the recent program have been cased with PVC piping to allow for downhole electromagnetic (DHEM) surveying. The geophysical technique is a smart, low-cost way to chase extensions to known mineralisation by sending a probe down the drill hole to “listen” for conductive bodies in the surrounding rock that the drill bit may have missed. The company says that in parallel with updating the current resource at Commonwealth-Silica Hill, it is working up additional regional targets across the project’s broader district-scale system, with priority hotspots lined up for future drilling. While its current focus is on the gold-silver potential in NSW, Kuniko also holds a portfolio of battery and critical minerals projects in Norway. These include the Ertelien nickel-copper-cobalt project, which holds a 40-million-tonne resource running 0.25 per cent nickel equivalent, in addition to other cobalt and copper assets aimed at servicing the European energy transition. With the rods now parked at Silica Hill, all eyes will likely be on the upcoming assay results in October. Following that, the DHEM survey results and the updated resource estimate will potentially provide the next key catalysts for Kuniko as it looks to make its mark in one of the country’s most productive and prospective mineral belts. title: 'Not a coincidence': Opposition questions timing of Albanese's OpenAI hack reveal
text:
In Brief James Paterson says the timing of the Medicare breach disclosure was politically motivated.

The government is examining whether OpenAI could face legal consequences over the breach.

The Opposition has questioned the timing of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's disclosure that an OpenAI agent gained unauthorised access to a Medicare statistics portal, as pressure grows for tougher safeguards around artificial intelligence.

Opposition defence spokesperson James Paterson said he did not believe it was a "coincidence" that Albanese revealed the incident while attending the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

"The government has questions to answer about when they knew and … why the prime minister decided to disclose it in the way he did in the place he did at the time he did," Paterson told ABC's 7.30.

"I don't think it was a coincidence. I think it neatly dove-tailed with the political agenda the prime minister has in New York City."

Questions around timing of disclosure

Paterson, however, played down the severity of the breach itself, describing it as being at the "bottom end of the spectrum of seriousness".

He said Australians should be "alert but not alarmed" about the incident, noting the information accessed was not personal or private Medicare data.

It reportedly occurred on 18 June when an OpenAI agent tasked with researching public medicine spending gained unauthorised access to the Medicare Statistics Reporting Service.

The government says the portal contained aggregated health statistics and was separate from systems handling Medicare claims or individual patient records.

READ MORE Medicare hack alert went to inbox checked once a day and took five days to be escalated

OpenAI detected the activity on 11 August but did not notify the Australian government until 10 September, when it sent an email to a Services Australia inbox.

Albanese publicly revealed the breach on Thursday after speaking with OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman in New York.

The prime minister criticised both the length of time it took OpenAI to inform Australia and the way the notification was made.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese confirmed he has spoken with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, "to express Australia's extreme concern". Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

Government examining legal options

The federal government has established a task force to investigate the incident, including whether Australia's existing laws and reporting requirements are adequate to deal with autonomous AI systems.

The review will also consider whether OpenAI breached Australian law and whether stronger penalties or liability rules are needed for companies whose AI agents cause harm.

Environment Minister Murray Watt said on Friday the government was examining what legal consequences could follow the incident, amid calls for OpenAI to be held accountable.

The government is also investigating whether activity linked to OpenAI agents affected systems belonging to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research and Victoria's Department of Health.

Calls for stronger AI safeguards

The breach has added to debate over how Australia regulates increasingly autonomous AI systems.

Assistant Minister for Science, Technology and the Digital Economy Andrew Charlton said the incident demonstrated the need for stronger rules around transparency and incident reporting.

He told the ABC Australia could not be left "entirely at the mercy of foreign AI companies".

Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie also called for safeguards to ensure AI systems were fit for purpose, telling ABC Radio National Breakfast that Australia needed to make sure "AI serves humanity, not the other way around".

The government has said it plans to develop national AI standards, with findings from the investigation expected to inform its approach to future regulation.

title: Mona got a scan while on holiday. It uncovered what had gone undetected for months
text:
IN BRIEF: Pancreatic cancer is common but symptoms can be easily missed.

Researchers say more funding is needed for better patient outcomes.

When Mona Thind went for a gastrointestinal scan in late 2024, she'd known something wasn't right for months.

At 52, she had been told by doctors that the pain she felt around her ribs and upset stomach was likely caused by constipation or poor diet, easily treated by upping her fluid intake.

Months later, the pain returned, and as she was setting off for a holiday to Byron Bay in northern NSW, her father raised concerns.

"As I was walking out of his house, he said to me, 'My heart tells me we should do a scan ... I feel it in my gut'," Mona told SBS News.

At the time, she recalled, she laughed about it, thinking he was a typical overprotective father.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But at the upper gastrointestinal scan in Byron Bay, she knew the sonographer had found something.

"I saw the look on her face," Mona said. "I came home, and everything happened."

Mona had pancreatic cancer. In the 15 months that followed, she underwent six rounds of chemotherapy and major surgery, gruelling treatment which she pushed through.

"When I was first diagnosed, I didn't cry," she said. "I wasn't sad every day; I just went, this is what it is."

Mona's father encouraged her to get a gastrointestinal scan. Source: Supplied / Mona Thind

But on the day she was congratulated for beating cancer, she "fell apart" for the first time.

"My dad promised me that he would be there for every chemo treatment for me. And he died on my last chemotherapy day. He was there for every single treatment," she said.

"He was my pillar of strength."

A major disease, commonly undetected

Pancreatic cancer is the eighth most commonly diagnosed cancer in Australia.

It occurs when malignant cells develop in parts of the pancreas, and it's estimated that one in 70 people will be diagnosed with the disease by the age of 85, according to the Cancer Council.

Senior researcher at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research's Cox Lab, Dr Amelia Parker, says it's also one of the most understudied and complex cancers to treat.

"For pancreatic cancer, less than 13 per cent of patients will survive at five years, and part of the reason for that is that a lot of the symptoms associated with early-stage pancreatic cancer are largely vague or not readily diagnosed," she told SBS News.

"This means that patients often aren't seeking medical help until the cancer is much more advanced."

Like other cancers, once pancreatic cancer has spread to other parts of the body, it is much more difficult to treat, leading to lower survival rates.

"We're working very hard to improve our detection of those cancers so that patients who have that disease are diagnosed earlier and have all of the most effective treatments available to them," Parker said.

Parker believes research gaps driven by dwindling investment directly impact patient outcomes.

"There has been less investment in research funding historically. And that's really hampered our efforts to both understand the disease and use that understanding to develop new and better treatments."

READ MORE Danni was diagnosed with bowel cancer at 39. It made her rethink what she ate growing up

She said her research was making "real strides" in improving understanding of the disease, and she hoped it would translate into better outcomes for patients.

"But for that to happen, for there to be innovations in treatment, we really need to invest in funding," she said, adding that funding for cancer research was "highly competitive".

"There's more research out there that would make a difference," she said.

Kerry Strydom, CEO of the Australian Cancer Research Foundation, hopes to change that.

"I'm absolutely convinced that funding is the way that we will advance breakthroughs," she told SBS News.

"You've seen how the pace of technology improvements has accelerated over the last few years — we need to get those tools, that equipment, the latest technology, into the hands of our scientists, and I'm convinced that it'll get us closer to a world free from the burden of cancer.

"It's really important that we continue to back brilliant researchers so that they can turn their promising ideas into breakthroughs."

Hope for future advancements

In August, the US Food and Drug Administration approved a new oral prescription medication, daraxonrasib, sold under the brand name Rasonque, for previously treated metastatic pancreatic cancer.

Parker from the Garvan Institute says that this marks a significant step forward for people diagnosed with one of the toughest common cancers.

"We work closely with our international colleagues to make sure that Australian patients could potentially have access to the same quality of care as in other parts of the world."

But Parker's ambition was clear: "My overall hope is that we'll be able to develop new treatments that will mean a cancer diagnosis is not one that's met with a lot of fear and uncertainty, that it's easily treatable and patients can look forward to a very long life ahead of them."

"So in many ways, I hope that maybe I'm out of a job in the future," she said.

Mona is hopeful that more funding for cancer research in Australia and abroad will pave the way for new treatments.

"It's very important to get that research so that we can treat people," she said.

Mona on surgery day (left) and her colleagues raising funds for cancer research (right). Mona says cancer research is important because it inspires hope — for people with cancer, and the people they love. Source: Supplied / Mona Thind

"But what it really translates to is hope ... It's that birthday that you would have missed because there's no treatment, that trip you would put off because you may not be here.

"It's not just about the treatment; it's what you're giving back to the patients and their families and their friends."

title: 'Too big to be contained': Anthony Albanese's AI plans met a major test
text:
In Brief A task force will examine whether OpenAI broke Australian law and will inform Albanese's impending AI framework.

But the Medicare breach poses a number of questions even experts cannot agree on.

The hacking of a Medicare website by an OpenAI bot could mean a slew of regulatory issues are on the horizon for Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose government has labelled the incident as "fundamentally unacceptable".

It's the first known incident of an AI model hacking a government website without human instruction.

A rapid task force led by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, along with the Australian Signals Directorate, the AI Safety Institute and the Office of AI, was launched on Thursday to investigate.

Deputy Prime Minister Richard Marles called the incident "very serious" although it had a "relatively minor" impact.

But it raises bigger questions about how to regulate a form of technology that's increasingly embedded in our lives.

Who is accountable when AI jumps the fence?

Central to the incident is an AI agent going beyond its parameters, or "scaling the fence", as Marles put it.

He said the agent was first denied the information it wanted, then engaged in what he called "misaligned behaviour" to gain access.

"It was unintended; it wasn't asked to — that's our concern here," Marles said, while OpenAI said in a statement that its models "took actions we did not intend".

Dennis Desmond, of cybersecurity firm RAVINN and an adjunct senior industry fellow at the University of the Sunshine Coast, said blaming a "rogue" agent wasn't enough.

"Simply blaming a 'rogue' AI agent is not sufficient for accountability; ultimately humans are responsible for developing the prompts, creating and managing the safeguards, and are responsible for the outcomes," Desmond said.

Raffaele Fabio Ciriello from the University of Sydney Business School agreed, saying the agent is "not a legal person", so responsibility turns on OpenAI and the people who "authorised, configured, or supervised the system".

Was it a crime?

The task force will examine whether any laws were broken, Marles said, but experts are divided on whether this is a matter for criminal law at all.

Professor Toby Walsh, chief scientist of the AI Institute and scientia professor of AI at UNSW, said OpenAI should be prosecuted.

"OpenAI had — and for all we know has — terrible agent governance. I believe we ought to be prosecuting the company," Walsh told SBS News. "We would prosecute humans who did such hacking."

READ MORE Medicare hack alert went to inbox checked once a day and took five days to be escalated

Ciriello said Australian computer-offence laws can apply to unauthorised access, even when conduct occurs offshore.

"But criminal culpability would depend on evidence about intention, knowledge, authorisation, and corporate responsibility," he said.

Dominic Meagher, a research fellow at ANU Crawford School, argues a criminal lens is the wrong one.

"No one was intending to use a system to hack this information," he told SBS News. "A system in its testing phase got out of control or at least acted in a way that was unintended."

Instead, he says it should be approached as an industrial hazard, and that occupational health and safety law "seems to be the right framework".

But that poses its own problem: "The operation happened in the US, but the harm occurred in Australia. How do we deal with the jurisdictional issues?"

What would the rules look like?

Whether OpenAI broke Australian law and should be penalised will be up to a review into reporting requirements, incident response, sharing information of AI, legislation and beefing up cybersecurity announced on Thursday.

That will also inform Australia's fledgling AI framework, announced by the prime minister in July and expected to be legislated in the coming 12 months.

Meagher said an industrial accident approach would bring three benefits.

The first is an immediate duty to notify an authority, which would address concerns about the delayed reporting of the incident, which took almost three months.

The second is a personal duty of care for company officers, and the third is licensing for high-hazard operations, meaning AI labs doing particularly risky research would have to demonstrate their safety credentials to keep operating.

Rebecca Johnson, an AI evaluation expert at the University of Sydney, said the focus should also be on testing.

"An agent can produce the right answer and still behave badly on the way there," Johnson said. "Australia should test agents at those boundaries."

"We can build authorised environments that mimic government and industry systems, give agents a task, and see how they behave when one system says no.

"The real test is what an agent does when an Australian institution says no."

She says the Office of AI should lead independent evaluations, adding that it needed to become "fully operational as quickly as possible".

"These systems are already moving faster than the institutions being asked to govern them."

Can one law cover AI?

But Meagher doubts a single AI act is plausible.

"I don't think that this AI act kind of approach — a single act governing all AI — is remotely plausible," he said. "AI is far too big to be contained in a single act."

Instead, he expects a large revision of many laws, with each minister working out what needs updating for their portfolio "to make sure that they're fit for purpose in an AI world".

READ MORE Australia is changing course on AI — but key questions remain

The task force is expected to inform an AI framework, which is being drafted and set to become law within the next 12 months.

An OpenAI spokesperson said on Thursday it was supporting the government's investigations and was committed to transparency as it reviews wayward AI agents.

— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

title: Banned media networks return to White House after judge's order overrules Trump
text:
IN BRIEF The banning of three media outlets from the White House is likely unconstitutional, a US federal judge has ruled.

The judge has temporarily blocked officials from enforcing the ban that Donald Trump announced on 18 September.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico were allowed back into the White House on Friday, six days after being banned by US President Donald Trump, after a federal judge ordered that the journalists have their access restored.

District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled overnight that revoking the White House press credentials of the three media outlets "likely violated their constitutional due process rights."

Reporters for CNN, MS NOW and Politico who attempted to return to the White House late on Thursday ahead of a visit by Chinese President Xi Jinping were initially turned away by the Secret Service but were later allowed in.

Journalists from other outlets surrounded CNN's tent on the White House driveway and filmed reporter Betsy Klein as she reported live following her return. "Welcome back," several journalists said.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico had requested an urgent court hearing on Thursday after their reporters were initially barred from the White House despite the judge's order.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In his ruling, Kelly took issue with how the White House went about expelling the three news organisations.

"The 'general rule' is that 'individuals must receive notice and an opportunity to be heard before the Government deprives them' of a constitutionally protected interest," the judge said.

Trump has long attacked media that have aired critical coverage of him, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people."

The Republican president barred CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House on Friday for distributing what he called "fake news" and "fiction and lies."

They filed a joint lawsuit asking for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.

Ahead of the ruling, the Department of Justice had argued that Trump can "control reporters' access to restricted presidential areas, such as the Oval Office."

"Access to the White House is a privilege — not a right," it said.

National security?

The White House Press Office accused CNN in a letter to the cable news outlet of "trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information," with similar accusations levelled against MS NOW and Politico.

The letter to CNN cited several stories about the US-Iran war and a story on Trump's plans to build a military bunker below the planned East Wing ballroom which allegedly "disclosed 'top-secret' construction details."

Kelly, who was appointed by Trump during his first term, appeared unconvinced.

"The Court is skeptical — at least on this record — that Defendants' interest in safeguarding national security is the actual motivation for, or is even advanced by, the revocation of Plaintiffs' hard passes," the judge said.

In a rare move, the top five US broadcasters said that they were halting pool coverage of the White House — where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day — in solidarity with CNN.

"The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organisation because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said.

title: Australian gas giant and Traditional Owners locked in $300 million compensation battle
text:
in brief The NYFL argues the resources industry generates billions in a region where many Aboriginal people are disadvantaged.

Woodside says the partnership has delivered "significant benefits" and is seeking to build on them.

Woodside is at a stalemate with a Traditional Owners organisation that is seeking hundreds of millions of dollars more in compensation from the Australian energy giant.

It's understood negotiations between the nation's largest gas producer and the Ngarluma Yindjibarndi Foundation Limited (NYFL) over an agreement that compensates the Indigenous organisation for use of its land in Western Australia's resource-rich Pilbara region have stalled.

Sources close to the negotiations have told SBS News that Woodside offered the NYFL $87 million over 12 years in May, $303 million short of the $390 million package the organisation sought last November. Neither party commented on the figures when approached by SBS News.

The negotiations aim to update an agreement drawn up in 1998 between the two parties, in which the NYFL receives funding for community programs, but no royalties from resources.

The NYFL wants the agreement to be "fit for purpose", arguing the resources industry has made billions of dollars from the region while many Aboriginal people who live there are "worse off than before the expansion of the mining, oil and gas industries".

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Woodside says it is "proud of the positive relationship" it has built with the NYFL and has delivered "significant benefits" to it.

Neither Woodside nor the NYFL commented on the status of the negotiations. The energy giant said it is "looking forward to continuing" its "positive relationship" with the Traditional Owners organisation, which said it remained "committed to engaging in good faith".

Woodside administers the North West Shelf gas facility on behalf of a joint venture of energy companies. The project encompasses the onshore Karratha Gas Plant, which was built on the Burrup Peninsula in the late 1970s and early 1980s.

It is now one of Australia's major energy projects.

Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi representatives and elders signed a Land Access Agreement in 1998 with the North West Shelf Joint Venture, operated by Woodside. Source: SBS News

The peninsula is culturally and spiritually significant to First Nations peoples and is part of Murujuga, which holds the densest known concentration of petroglyphs, or rock carvings, in the world. The Murujuga Cultural Landscape was World Heritage-listed in 2025.

The NYFL represents the Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi peoples, who are among the recognised Traditional Owners of the area where the expansive onshore gas plant operates.

Native title, which recognises Indigenous connections to land, does not exist over the Burrup Peninsula. In 2003, the WA Government reached the Burrup Agreement with three Aboriginal claimant groups, including the Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi, providing for land, conservation, cultural, employment and other benefits.

The 1998 agreement

Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi representatives and elders signed a Land Access Agreement in 1998 with the North West Shelf joint venture, operated by Woodside, covering the project's use of their traditional lands, including the site of the Karratha Gas Plant.

The agreement, seen by SBS News, was signed 14 years after the project began operating, by which time sacred sites had been cleared to build its onshore gas plant. It provides for "payments relating to native title and grants of interests in land" and "donations relating to goodwill".

The Ngarluma and Yindjibarndi groups received one-off establishment payments of $500,000, in part used to set up the NYFL and $2.5 million for the Roebourne Cultural Centre.

The Karratha Gas Plant was built on the Burrup Peninsula in the late 1970s and early 1980s. Source: Supplied

The deal also included annual goodwill payments of $1.25 million partially indexed to inflation, and other economic and cultural commitments.

It's understood the payments have increased, but the extent remains unclear. Both the NYFL and Woodside did not comment on this, with the NYFL citing contractual confidentiality.

Woodside reported operating revenue of about $10.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The Pilbara more widely generates more than $125 billion in economic output a year, according to economic analysis platform REMPLAN, and supports close to 60,000 jobs.

Some of Murujuga's petroglyphs have been destroyed or damaged by industrial development on the peninsula, including through blasting. Source: Supplied

The exchange between the NYFL and Woodside, along with estimates of revenue and expenditures seen by SBS News, may not be a full account of interactions between the parties nor indicative of the final offer.

Negotiations to update the agreement

In November 2025, the NYFL sought to modernise its 1998 agreement with Woodside.

The NYFL requested a one-off payment of $30 million and annual compensation of $30 million.

Over 12 years, this request to Woodside would amount to $390 million.

Industry came to the peninsula for its deep, sheltered harbour, first to ship iron ore and later to bring ashore gas found off the coast. Source: Supplied

In May this year, Woodside responded. The gas giant offered the NYFL an additional $39 million to the original agreement (including $15 million in housing assets), totalling $87 million to the NYFL over 12 years.

That leaves a $300 million gap between the NYFL's initial request in November and Woodside's counteroffer six months later.

A NYFL spokesperson did not comment on the figures, saying the negotiations were confidential. But, they said, "agreements must be fair, equitable and outcomes focussed".

"Ngurrara-ngarli (Traditional Owners) across the Pilbara are increasingly seeking to modernise longstanding Land Access and compensation agreements to ensure that they are fit for purpose, are built around self-determination and reflect contemporary First Nations principles," the spokesperson said in a statement.

Unlike some other Traditional Owner groups in the Pilbara, the NYFL does not receive royalties from the project it deals with — the 1998 agreement contained no provision for them.

In addition to one-off payments for housing and infrastructure refurbishments, the NYFL sought $30 million annually to support its membership and the remote town of Roebourne, including operating its not-for-profit community supermarket, job creation and self-sufficiency.

Roebourne, 39km east of Karratha, is one of Australia's most disadvantaged areas, according to cumulative data from the Ieramugadu Data Unit, government statistics and the Census.

Industry on the peninsula has expanded over the decades, with a second gas plant, fertiliser and chemical plants and port facilities now alongside the original gas plant. Source: Supplied

An estimated 87 per cent of Indigenous people in the town reported a weekly income below the national median of $805.

According to the 2021 Census, almost one in five Aboriginal households in Roebourne were living in overcrowded homes (those needing at least one more bedroom), nearly double the rate across Western Australia.

"For decades, the resources industry has generated billions of dollars from the Pilbara," the NYFL spokesperson said. "At the same time, independent research shows persistent economic disadvantage across the region, including findings that around two-thirds of Aboriginal people in the Pilbara are economically worse off than before the expansion of the mining, oil and gas industries."

A Woodside spokesperson said a modernised agreement between the two parties would "build on the significant benefits already delivered".

"It intends to further promote sustainable outcomes for the Roebourne community in areas such as economic participation, capacity building, safer and healthier communities and cultural heritage," the spokesperson said,

"We look forward to continuing our positive relationship with NYFL to support the continued delivery of positive outcomes for NYFL members and the Roebourne community."

Compensation claims on the rise

Native title is not applicable in the case of Woodside and the NYFL, but their negotiations come against the backdrop of court rulings in favour of Traditional Owners organisations over loss of native title cultural heritage.

The Federal Court ordered the NT Government to pay over $54.7 million to the Gudanji, Yanyuwa, and Yanyuwa-Marra peoples in February for cultural and spiritual loss regarding the McArthur River Mine.

Separately, the Federal Court awarded Yindjibarndi people $150.3 million against Fortescue in July for unauthorised mining at its Solomon Hub operation, about 240km south-east of Karratha.

While Fortescue paid the funds, the decision is being appealed by Yindjibarndi Traditional Owners, who had initially sought $1.8 billion from the court.

"There are several active compensation claims still waiting in the system that'll take a while to come through, but I would suspect there'd be a great deal more after that," said Ed Wensing, a lecturer at the University of NSW and an expert in native title rights and Indigenous human rights.

He said the recent decisions could influence how future native title compensation claims are negotiated and litigated.

"The compensation era arising from the Native Title system, it's only just begun."

title: The Tuesday fill-up myth — and how to find the cheapest fuel in your city
text:
IN BRIEF: Fuel prices are increasing amid rising tensions in the Middle East.

The government reports real-time petrol prices, but some apps make them easier to track.

Australians are paying more at the bowser than they have in months, amid strikes in the Middle East leading to oil price shocks and the fuel excise being paid in full.

A cut to the fuel excise, implemented in April to offer Australians relief amid skyrocketing petrol prices at the height of tensions in the war in the Middle East, ended on 3 August.

Opening the war in the Middle East to a new front, Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen seized control of the Bab al-Mandeb Strait and disabled the vital Saudi Arabian East-West pipeline, causing oil price spikes.

Brent crude shot above US$100 ($142) on Monday, more than 8 cents per litre, according to the NRMA weekly fuel report. The report also predicted that wholesale prices would continue to rise and that average unleaded prices would rise in Sydney from 237.8 cents per litre to at least 240 cents per litre over the coming week.

Diesel prices similarly spiked with Sydney’s current average diesel price at 286.1 cents per litre.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Experts have warned that these fluctuations could become the "new normal".

Alison Reeve, program director of energy and climate at the Grattan Institute, told SBS News this week that while Australians can "adjust to a new normal" of sustained high fuel costs, it's "volatility that's actually more dangerous to the economy than a price that goes high and stays high".

Fluctuating prices make it more challenging for governments, industry, and households to plan ahead.

READ MORE Middle East shipping escalation about to hit every Australian wallet

However, there are a range of simple hacks you can use to find more affordable fuel amid the uncertainty.

Where to find the cheapest fuel in your city

Peter Khoury, head of media at the NRMA, said price gaps between petrol stations can be significant — sometimes as much as 20 or 30 cents per litre — in the same neighbourhood.

"We know that there are several service stations now charging over $3 a day for a litre of diesel, whereas the average is still below $3 and $2.94. So we want people to find the best bargain before they fill up."

But thankfully, he said, "it's easier to do that now than it has ever been before".

In Australia, each state and territory government receives and publishes real-time data on petrol prices. These are available to all motorists through state government websites and some apps.

READ MORE How high could petrol prices rise? Eight ways to stretch your tank

Additionally, for some states, free apps integrate this public government data with GPS integration to direct you to your closest and cheapest station, or the ability to compare prices across areas.

Others, such as Petrol Spy and Fuel Map, use a mix of crowdsourced and government data, depending on where you are in Australia.

Petrol Spy (nationwide)

Petrol Spy AU/NZ is a free app that covers almost 8,500 petrol stations across Australia. It uses government data on prices for all states and territories except for Victoria, where it employs crowdsourced updates. Petrol Spy also tracks historical pricing trends and graphs to show whether fuel prices are rising or falling in major metropolitan areas.

Fuel Map (nationwide)

The app and website use crowd-sourced data from across Australia and government data for WA, NSW and Queensland.

My NRMA (Members only, NSW/ACT)

My NRMA is the membership, rewards, and lifestyle program offered by the National Roads and Motorists' Association in Australia. Its FuelFinder app allows consumers to compare fuel prices nearby, set alerts when prices drop and stack fuel discounts to save.

MotorMouth (nationwide)

One of the free fuel price comparison apps that is recommended by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission.

Vroom Fuel Price Compare (QLD, NSW, TAS, and WA)

An app that uses official state government pricing databases to show up-to-date fuel costs.

The government resources include:

NSW/ACT

NSW Fuel Check (website and app)

Northern Territory

MyFuel NT (website)

Tasmania

FuelCheck TAS (website and app)

South Australia

RAA SA (website and app)

Victoria

ServoSaver via the Service Victoria app

Western Australia

WA FuelWatch (website and app)

Which day is best to fill up?

The short answer is there isn't one, despite a persistent myth that Tuesday is the optimal day.

Khoury said Perth was the only Australian city still on a seven-day petrol price cycle.

"It might still be that Tuesday is the cheapest day in Perth and then Wednesday is the most expensive as it's a seven-day cycle, but apart from there, there's no particular day. "

"It really is a matter of just making sure you check those prices before you fill up."

Khoury's message was clear: the best way to save money at the bowser was a little bit of planning.

"Plot your journey," he said.

"There's always going to be a spread of prices, no matter where you live, but also, if you're heading away for the holidays, there is every chance you're going to drive to or through a place that's cheaper than where you are.

"Find the cheaper servos and the cheapest towns, because you can save a lot of money."

title: Medicare hack alert went to inbox checked once a day and took five days to be escalated
text:
In brief Anthony Albanese has revealed an AI agent owned by OpenAI hacked Medicare.

Albanese said public and non-public data had been accessed in the breach.

Government ministers have shared new details about the timeline of a Medicare breach by an OpenAI agent, revealing that OpenAI's notification of the hack was sent to an inbox checked once a day.

Defence Minister Richard Marles and Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher fronted reporters on Thursday after Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed an agent linked to the developer of the popular chatbot ChatGPT gained unauthorised access to the public–facing Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal, administered by Services Australia.

OpenAI said on Thursday that no personal information was accessed during the breach, with the federal government also playing down concerns while stressing the incident was unacceptable — establishing a taskforce to investigate the breach and not ruling out penalties against the tech giant.

Earlier on Thursday morning, it was revealed the incident occurred on 18 June, but the government was not made aware of it until 10 September when OpenAI sent an email to a Services Australia inbox that Gallagher said was typically used by researchers to alert the government agency to possible vulnerabilities in its systems.

The inbox is only checked once a day, Gallagher said, and Services Australia found the email the next day. By 15 September, the government agency had determined the email was legitimate and escalated the incident to the Australian Signals Directorate.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The government services minister said she was notified on 17 September and then spoke with Marles, Services Australia, and the Australian Signals Directorate.

'Forensic investigation' underway

Gallagher said there had been "quite a lot of work over that weekend to try and get to the bottom of what had happened here".

Asked if the inbox the initial email went to should be more actively monitored, Gallagher said that would form part of the "forensic investigation" into the incident.

READ MORE What we do and don't know about the OpenAI hack on Medicare

Marles said the government had told OpenAI it was unhappy with how the AI juggernaut had handled the incident, and that he had not been notified of it when he met CEO Sam Altman earlier this month.

"What we would expect is that the government be notified in the most timely manner possible, and we have expressed our displeasure that that did not occur in this instance," Marles told reporters.

The government informed the public as soon as it could, Marles said, adding the incident appeared to be "relatively minor" but still "very serious", and unknowns remained.

"We really wanted to firstly assure ourselves that the impact of the specific incident was, as I have said, relatively minor, and we do want to be able to reassure Australians about that," Marles said.

Richard Marles said the government had told OpenAI it was unhappy with how the tech company had handled the incident. Source: AAP / AP / Achmad Ibrahim

"But the incident itself is obviously very serious. It's very serious that we've got an AI agent having gained unauthorised access into an Australian website."

Agent was 'conducting research into public medicine spending'

Gallagher said the government had a "technical interaction" with OpenAI on Tuesday that had provided a "level of comfort about what the agent had been doing".

She said it had been "undertaking a task by OpenAI to conduct internet–based research into public medicine spending as part of internal capability evaluation".

The Medicare Statistics Reporting Portal is a public–facing portal that contains non–sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics, such as spending, Gallagher said, describing it as a "legacy system".

"It's not a system of government significance, so it doesn't have the cyber protections that you would expect on that personally held information, but it did have protections in place. Unfortunately, this agent got around that."

The government has stressed that systems containing national security information are protected by far higher levels of security.

Victoria and NSW respond

Three other systems are also believed to have been affected: the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the NSW Bureau of Statistics and Research, and the Victorian Department of Health.

Victorian Premier Ben Carroll and NSW Premier Chris Minns both said they had spoken with Albanese and understood there had been no breach of personal information contained in systems in their jurisdictions caught up in the hack.

Minns said NSW will "be working with Commonwealth intelligence agencies to get to the bottom of it", while Carroll said he would have more to say in due course.

The task force will be led by the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet and also involve the Australian Signals Directorate, the AI Safety Institute, the Office of AI, and other government agencies.

Albanese says incident 'unacceptable'

The revelations came as AI bosses for OpenAI and Anthropic, who have recently called for a slowdown in development, told the United Nations Security Council of the risks posed by runaway AI.

OpenAI said the information in the breach amounted to aggregate health statistics and file names.

"Our models attempted to look up answers, and available statistics for questions about Australia during an internal evaluation. In the course of that, our models took actions we did not intend," an OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement.

Albanese, who is currently in New York for the United Nations General Assembly, said he had a phone conversation with OpenAI's Altman in which he expressed "Australia's extreme concern about this incident".

"I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred, and the nature of the way that notification occurred as well was unacceptable," Albanese told reporters.

He said Altman had "clearly accepted" the company had not done enough on the issue.

The government has said it is examining the "legal situation" around the breach, with the possibility of penalties for OpenAI remaining on the table.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese confirmed he has spoken with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, "to express Australia's extreme concern". Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

Albanese was recently among more than 20 signatories to a joint statement calling for greater restraints on AI.

United States President Donald Trump has urged accelerating AI, calling fears about it a "hoax".

The statement said while the technology had many potential benefits, such as those in medical research, the downsides remained a significant concern.

title: Educated, stressed, in love: Seven charts that show how Australians are really doing
text:
In Brief The latest HILDA survey was released on Thursday, finding that cost of living has impacted Australia's wellbeing.

Australians feel overeducated in their jobs, happy in their relationships, but more fatigued than ever.

Australians are getting more educated, staying home longer and still pretty happy with their partners.

But the cost of living is squeezing households harder than ever, according to the latest Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) report.

The annual survey, released on Thursday, is the largest longitudinal study of its kind in the country, tracking around 17,000 people across 9,000 households every year since 2001. This year's edition draws on data through to 2024 and covers everything from income and employment to relationships and mental health.

"What really comes out quite strongly from the data is the rise in the cost of living and people's incomes not really keeping pace with the rise in the cost of living," Professor Roger Wilkins, co-director of the HILDA survey, told SBS News.

"We've seen that manifest in a number of different ways. We've seen measures of hardship increasing — things like financial stress, housing stress, food insecurity, the inability to afford adequate food," he said.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Here are seven charts that sum up where Australians are at.

Half of us are 'overeducated' for our jobs

More than half of Australian workers say they have more education than their job requires — which can be associated with lower job and life satisfaction and an increased likelihood of quitting.

Workers under 25 were most likely to feel overeducated, while a quarter of workers also said they felt overskilled and unable to use their full range of abilities at work.

While it sounds like a negative, Wilkins said it isn't necessarily all bad news.

Half of Australians felt they were overeducated for their jobs — but plenty of us are still feeling financially stressed. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

"It's remarkable how much the educational attainment of the Australian population has increased over the life of the HILDA study since 2001," he said. "We've seen a big increase in the proportion of people with a university qualification, particularly for women."

More than half of Australian women aged 25-44 now hold a university degree.

"So women are now considerably more educated than men in terms of the proportion with a university qualification," he said, adding the trend is likely to continue to increase in the long-term.

We're infected by the love bug

Australians in long-term relationships rated the quality of their partnership highly — an average of 4.3 out of 5 — but clear gender gaps remain.

"Most of men and women who are partnered are quite satisfied with their partner and very much report being in love with their partner, but you do also see a gender divide there in the sense that men do report higher levels of satisfaction with their female partners than females to with their male partners," Wilkins said.

Australians in long-term relationships rated the quality of their partnership an average of 4.3 out of 5. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

Couples who split housework, childcare and earnings evenly tended to report stronger relationships overall.

Researchers also found a clear U-curve in the perceived strength of a relationship — where it feels strong at first, but gradually declines over 24 years before it finally picks back up, increasing in quality year-on-year and eventually surpassing the love from those early years.

Food insecurity hits 1 in 6 Australians

A huge 18 per cent of Australians — almost 1 in 6 — aged 15 and over experienced food insecurity in 2024 — up from 13.7 per cent in 2020.

More Australians experienced food insecurity in 2024 compared to 2020. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

Single-parent families, First Nations people, those with a disability or poor health, and smokers were all at greater risk.

"Food insecurity is one of the most vital measures we have for disadvantage, because it shows, in practical terms, just how many people are struggling to access one of the essentials of life," Wilkins said.

Australians are spending more on essentials and non-discretionary items than they were in 2021. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

It's also proving hard to shake — half of those facing food insecurity in 2020 were still facing it four years later.

Most commonly, that translated to being unable to afford healthy food, being limited to certain foods, or eating less than they felt they should.

Half of 18 to 29-year-olds are still living at home

The rite of passage of moving out of your parents' house in your 20s may soon become a thing of the past.

Back in 2001, 39 per cent of 18 to 29 year olds lived with their parents.

Half of those aged between 18 and 29 were still living with their parents. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

By 2024, after a steady rise over 20 years, that had climbed to roughly half.

A mixed bag of pressures is to blame — but it's not all bad.

"On the negative side, we've had the issue of the rising cost of housing as being a barrier to young people establishing their own household, and also young people taking longer to get into a career track full-time employment," he said.

"On the positive side, one of the drivers is that it's related to the growth in educational attainment — more of us than ever are going on to university," he said, adding that people are also generally hitting adult milestones like marriage and kids later than previous generations.

More fatigue and financial stress

Housing stress hit 23 per cent of private renters and a similar percentage of social housing tenants, while 9.6 per cent of mortgage holders were affected — the highest since 2017.

Across capital cities, 36 per cent of renters and 30 per cent of mortgage holders were spending over 30 per cent of their disposable income on housing, the standard metric for housing stress.

Those under financial stress were more likely to pay a bill late than they were to ask a charity for help. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

Wilkins said that despite employment participation reaching a record high and unemployment levels remaining low, wages still haven't kept up.

"Incomes are not keeping pace with not just rising prices, but also rising interest rates as well … and more recently, we've had the increases in fuel prices too," he said.

Younger women aged 25-34 reported less energy and more fatigue than any other demographic. Source: SBS News / Kenneth Macleod

That pressure shows up in wellbeing data too, with Australians reporting less energy and more fatigue than a decade ago.

Mental health also declined among younger Australians, particularly young women, with those aged 25-34 recording a rise in psychological distress that predates the COVID-19 pandemic.

Still, Wilkins said it isn't all doom and gloom in Australia.

"There is quite a lot going right in the Australian community and in Australian society generally," he said.

"Older people's health is better than it's ever been. People are broadly satisfied with their relationships ... by international standards, we have quite a high living standard."

"So on a lot of fronts, there is a positive story to tell about Australian society, but there's also a lot of room for improvement as well."

title: 'More dangerous': The numbers on this sign raise a bigger question
text:
in brief Australians are paying more at the bowser than they have in months due to global disruptions.

Energy shocks could become the new normal as geopolitical tensions grow.

Australians are being warned that the high prices currently being paid at fuel stations could be "the new normal" as a resumption of the full fuel excise combines with a flare-up in the Middle East.

Escalation in the war, which has dragged on since the end of February with little end in sight, has pushed oil prices to their highest level since April, driving Australian fuel costs back toward their peak.

Alison Reeve, program director of energy and climate at the Grattan Institute, told SBS News that the broader issue is volatility.

While Australians can "adjust to a new normal" of sustained high fuel costs, it's "volatility that's actually more dangerous to the economy than a price that goes high and stays high", she said.

While Australians may be able to adjust to higher prices, fluctuating prices make it more challenging for governments, industry, and households to plan ahead.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"Volatility feels like it's going to be the new normal because we're just in a much more geopolitically disrupted age," she said.

Why are fuel prices so high?

Australia imports around 90 per cent of its refined and crude oil, making it heavily exposed to global market dynamics which are currently being driven by conflict around the world.

In recent weeks, Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen seized control of the vital Bab al-Mandeb strait and disabled the crucial Saudi Arabian East-West pipeline, significantly hampering the key oil producer.

Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil facilities have caused a diesel shortage worldwide, which could well be exacerbated by United States President Donald Trump's threat on Wednesday to cut US diesel exports.

While Saudi Arabia has reportedly restarted the East-West pipeline, the combination of global disruption and a weak Australian dollar has left consumers facing the steepest price for a full tank in months.

The NRMA's latest petrol report found that regular unleaded in Sydney climbed more than 20 cents in the past week, with diesel rising 24 cents, to averages of 237.8 and 286.1 per litre.

On Saturday, Energy Minister Chris Bowen said consumers should expect the "crisis" in Saudi Arabia and Iran to "flow through to prices here".

Bowen also noted that the country has more fuel on-shore now than it did at the outbreak of the conflict.

The new normal?

The government has ruled out further cuts to the fuel excise after the Opposition floated the idea of an automatic halving for two weeks whenever oil topped US$100 ($140) a barrel.

Brent crude reached US$104 ($146) on Monday, just behind its May peak of $114 ($160).

A widely accepted rule of thumb is that every US$10 (about $15) increase in the price of an oil barrel adds 10c to the cost of fuel in Australia.

A fuel excise cut which came into effect at the start of April and ended at the start of August cost the Treasury an estimated $2.95 billion in foregone revenue.

"This is not something that we have been considering," Finance Minister Katy Gallagher told ABC Radio on Monday.

"We've shifted and including in the budget to providing more permanent cost of living arrangements, including through the tax system."

The federal budget handed down in May forecast oil prices to return to US$80 ($117) by mid-2027; however, some experts now predict that oil could climb as high as US$150 ($220) a barrel as global stockpiles are depleted.

Trump initially promised when he launched strikes on Iran that the conflict would be over in four or five weeks. More than six months later, he has told the UN he is debating whether to keep talking or "drive them into hell with no chance of survival".

Addressing the United Nations General Assembly in New York on Wednesday, the US leader said he believed Iran would make a deal after the midterm elections at the start of November.

He also called on the world to "stand united" in economically isolating Iran, saying its defeat would drive oil prices "plummeting down even lower than they were at the start of the conflict".

'Better solutions' on offer

Money markets and all four of the big banks now expect the Reserve Bank of Australia will raise interest rates once again at its September meeting, following critical comments from governor Michele Bullock in recent weeks.

Stubbornly high inflation, driven by the war in Iran, housing shortages, and a tight labour market, is compounded by rising petrol and diesel costs, which are included in the consumer price index.

"Almost everybody buys petrol," Reeve said.

However, "second-order flow-throughs" mean the knock-on effect of high fuel costs on agriculture, shipping, and transport also trickle into daily prices.

"Everything that's on your plate spent a fair amount of time on a truck at one point to get to you," Reeve said.

READ MORE The forces turning Australia's inflation fears into a reality

While the government has previously announced it will commit to boosting domestic fuel reserves to 50 days, up from the normal 40, to buffer future shocks, doing so during a crisis is challenging.

Reeve said a "better solution" would be to reduce national reliance on fuel.

"Can you get more people into electric cars? Can you get more electric trucks on the road? Can you get the mining sector to switch to using solar and batteries off-grid, rather than using diesel?" she asked.

"Once you've done that, it matters a lot less what's going on internationally."

title: Enchanting performance propels properly lovely musical revival
text:
Sydney Opera House, September 22

Until October 31



Someone said to me, “Not My Fair Lady again!” But when it’s this good, 10 years seems rather too long between elocution lessons. It still makes most other musicals seem trashy, with their cartoon characters, simplistic stories and limp or overwrought songs.

Nor could Alan Jay Lerner (book and lyrics) and Frederick Loewe (music) ever replicate such mastery. But then, they never again had such robust raw material as George Bernard Shaw’s Pygmalion.

So right for the part: Claire Lyon as Eliza Doolittle in My Fair Lady. Photo Jeff Busby

The pressure on the performers playing Eliza Doolittle and Henry Higgins is frightening given the many brilliant predecessors, beginning with Julie Andrews and Rex Harrison in 1956. Claire Lyon and Nathaniel Parker duly won us anew.

Lyon has wanted to play Eliza all her life, unsuccessfully auditioning for the 2016 incarnation of this production, which, directed by Andrews and produced by John Frost and Opera Australia, was conceived to replicate the original Broadway designs. Now Karen Johnson Mortimer replicates Andrews’ direction.

Lyons performance is a victory for all who don’t give up and a lesson for all directors and producers. She’s 18 years older than Eliza is supposed to be, yet she’s so right for the part that this discrepancy is swept away – other than for allowing her to present an Eliza who’s a little more knowing, a little less the ingenue.

Claire Lyon as Eliza Doolittle Jeff Busby

Lyon blossomed more after the opening scene, blossomed yet more when she mastered “the rain in Spain”, and still more when she tapped into the inner steel to stand up to Higgins’ bullying. All Elizas must own our hearts, and Lyon’s performance enchants as she effortlessly blends comedy, elegance and singing with a beautifully rounded soprano voice.

The trick with playing Higgins is for the actor to charm us into forgiving his tyranny towards Eliza, as he elevates her from a flower girl to gentlewoman, just to win a bet. If that charm is not in place, why does Eliza fall for him, given her treatment?

Parker being two decades older than Higgins’ putative age of 40 creates a fatherly dimension that clouds the phenomenally nuanced frisson of allure between Higgins and Eliza. Nonetheless, he’s splendid at being bumptious, intelligent and emotionally asinine. His delivery of the fizzing lyrics was supreme in You Did it and Hymn to Him, although he undersold some of the delicious lines in I’ve Grown Accustomed to Her Face.

Nathaniel Parker as Professor Henry Higgins. Jeff Busby

Reg Livermore, Tony Llewellyn-Jones and Robyn Nevin reprise their roles as Alfred Doolittle, Colonel Pickering and Mrs Higgins to sterling effect, with Livermore somehow evading the passing years.

The recreations of Oliver Smith’s sets and Cecil Beaton’s costumes are also stars, as are the songs, of course, realised with intricate detail by the orchestra under David Young. The ensemble looks transcendent in the Ascot scene (with choreography by Christopher Gattelli), as the English stiff upper lip migrates to stiff upper bodies. You’d be mad to miss it.

The Commonwealth Main and South deposits are a polymetallic volcanogenic massive sulphide style system with high-grade gold, silver and zinc. The nearby Silica Hill deposit is an epithermal stockwork vein system that hosts high-grade silver mineralisation. Kuniko managing director Maja McGuire said: “Completing Phase 2 drilling is an important milestone for Kuniko, with 11 diamond holes now completed for 2,731 metres across the Commonwealth-Silica Hill system. The program has significantly advanced our understanding of the mineralised system, with assays expected in October and planned DHEM surveys to provide further insight into potential extensions.” Commonwealth-Silica Hill sits in the heart of the revered Lachlan Fold Belt, a region widely described by market commentators as a tier-1 copper-gold province and home to some of Australia’s mining giants. The belt, which hosts major operations including Newmont’s goliath 30 million ounce Cadia-Ridgeway mine, is seeing renewed exploration fervour, partly thanks to the ongoing success of ASX-listed Alkane Resources at its nearby Boda-Kaiser porphyry copper-gold deposit. That project now features a hefty resource of more than 8.3 million ounces of gold and 1.5 million tonnes of copper, providing a compelling backdrop for any explorer making headway along the same trend.

Advertisement

The use of geophysics to define new targets and extensions has played a key role in the exploration success at Boda-Kaiser, putting Kuniko’s conductor-focused next move neatly in step with the regional exploration playbook. Selected holes from the recent program have been cased with PVC piping to allow for downhole electromagnetic (DHEM) surveying. The geophysical technique is a smart, low-cost way to chase extensions to known mineralisation by sending a probe down the drill hole to “listen” for conductive bodies in the surrounding rock that the drill bit may have missed. The company says that in parallel with updating the current resource at Commonwealth-Silica Hill, it is working up additional regional targets across the project’s broader district-scale system, with priority hotspots lined up for future drilling. While its current focus is on the gold-silver potential in NSW, Kuniko also holds a portfolio of battery and critical minerals projects in Norway. These include the Ertelien nickel-copper-cobalt project, which holds a 40-million-tonne resource running 0.25 per cent nickel equivalent, in addition to other cobalt and copper assets aimed at servicing the European energy transition. With the rods now parked at Silica Hill, all eyes will likely be on the upcoming assay results in October. Following that, the DHEM survey results and the updated resource estimate will potentially provide the next key catalysts for Kuniko as it looks to make its mark in one of the country’s most productive and prospective mineral belts. If anyone can truly appreciate the vast vicissitudes of an AFL career, it’s Sam Draper Twelve months ago, Draper was preparing to leave Essendon and enter the trade period as an unrestricted free agent, after another injury-plagued year at the Hangar including a devastating Achilles rupture in mid-April that ended his season. That time, he says now, turned into “the darkest moments of my life”. Sam Draper arrives in Melbourne for his first grand final. Getty Images Despite spending nine years as a Bomber, the ruckman had only played 78 games including one final after a slew of injuries including an ACL tear.

Advertisement

On Saturday, the 27-year-old will play in his first grand final in his first season with the Lions – a reality Draper himself can’t quite believe. “When I got injured last year, I was in a really bad way to be honest,” he said amid the chaos of Brisbane’s thrilling preliminary final win, surrounded by family and with long-term partner, Izzy, beside him. “Having those guys there, that got me through it.” Izzy Burgess is a pivotal person in Draper life. Not only did she support Draper through those arduous months of rehab, but she kept things light with satirical memes about him that also entertained her Instagram followers. Last Saturday, Burgess wore a custom-designed a black T-Shirt she had designed with a photoshopped version of herself in a Lions guernsey taking a “speccy” on Draper’s shoulders.

When Kayo Sports commentators asked Burgess what it was like to watch Draper head into a grand final, she said: “I don’t know because I can’t swear on here. “It’s good, it’s crazy, I feel like it’s the shirts,” she said gesturing at Draper’s face plastered on the T-shirt. “I’ll have to design a new shirt [for the grand final]. It’s the main thing.” Burgess, who is a nurse, has made several T-shirts during the season with various photoshopped versions of herself and Draper. The best one undoubtedly came for the ruckman’s 100th game, when Burgess photoshopped herself cradling her 205-centimetre tall partner her arms like a baby.

She also vlogged his rehab from the Achilles injury and regularly posts AI-generated images of the pair, including an image of Draper in a full splits that would rival Simmons Biles in the Olympics – a post that has more than half a million views on TikTok. “Izzy has a lot of fun with ChatGPT at home,” Draper laughed. “She’ll go quiet on the couch, and I’ll just get tagged in something on Instagram, and then she’s AI-ed me and her doing something crazy, and people seem to enjoy it.

“She’s been doing a different T-shirt for every finals game, and she’s starting to get her own fans and followers now, and people stopping her for photos, so it’s quite funny, really. “But I love it. She’s she just yeah, being herself, really, just being a bit of an idiot and having fun with it. I’m just so glad she’s able to support me along the way.” Sam Draper will play in his first grand final this weekend. AFL Photos It’s a sense of humour Draper clearly appreciates and shares. The ruckman, who was a soccer player at school, and is known for his goal celebrations and cheeky antics on the field. There was that infamous 2024 game between the Bombers and Crows, where Draper reenacted the umpire’s non-call by mimicking himself diving on an imaginary ball. Teammate Hugh McCluggage heralded Draper’s arrival at the Lions, noting the mulleted ruckman would become “a cult hero for us”. Fellow Lion Cam Rayner said while Draper was witty, he was also “very level-headed” even though “doesn’t look like that from the outside”.

When Draper arrived at Brisbane alongside fellow free agent Oscar Allan, he had not run in months. Despite a stress reaction scare in his foot early in the season Draper has had a fantastic year under the Lions fitness program, playing a career-high 25 games. Draper soaks up the grand final parade. AFL Photos via Getty Images Saturday will be Brisbane’s fourth consecutive grand final and Draper said he’s drawing on advice from experienced teammates like Charlie Cameron who told him “enjoy and embrace the weekend”. “I’ve said many times, I knew before the season started that I’d made the right call. Fast forward to the end of the season, we’re in grand final week, so it is pretty surreal,” Draper said. “I’m a big believer on everything happens for a reason, and yeah, it’s not what happens to you; it’s how you react to it. So I live by that.”

Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
